meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 16, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: In a pivotal budget meeting, the Durham City Council voted 4-3 on a substitute motion by Steve Schewel (with Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden dissenting) to repeal the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replace it with a property tax increase, and then adopted the remaining FY 2014-15 budget and CIP ordinances 6-1 (with Eugene Brown dissenting over the final budget's inclusion of the fee repeal). Council also unanimously approved a $100,000 incentive grant for Reinvestment Partners' North Mangum Street food hub, the New Hope Church Transportation Special Use Permit and major site plan, a $74,985 Riverside on the Eno stormwater reimbursement, concealed-carry park ordinance updates conforming to state law, and accepted City Manager Tom Bonfield's 60-day review plan for the 44 HRC and CPRB police recommendations.

agenda_items.title: Parks & Recreation Month, DPD Forensics ISO Accreditation, Linda Bratcher Retirement, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented resolutions for Parks and Recreation Month and the Durham Police Department Forensics Services Division's ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation. Council members also recognized retiring staff member Linda Bratcher and praised Steve Schewel's Durham News op-ed on city taxes.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Item 33 Order, Supplemental Item 36, and HRC/CPRB Memo)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield moved Item 33 after Item 32, added supplemental Item 36 (Riverside on the Eno CIP ordinance amendment), and added his review/timeline memo on the Human Relations Commission and Civilian Police Review Board recommendations to the public record.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Excluding Pulled Items 10 and 11)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda excluding Item 10 (FY15 Budget) and Item 11 (Concealed carry ordinance), encompassing numerous board/commission appointments, transportation grant amendments, WIA youth contracts, Downtown Durham MSD and DDI FY15 agreements, Balfour Beatty City Hall/Annex envelope CMAR contract, street repairs, Safe Routes to School near Fayetteville St. Elementary, and water tank/Jordan Lake contracts.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City Code Section 38-21 (Alcoholic Beverages in Parks / McCown-Mangum House)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Patrick Baker presented an ordinance amendment permitting permitted alcohol consumption on the lawn of the McCown-Mangum House at West Point on the Eno Park consistent with other city park facilities. Speaker Victoria Peterson argued against allowing alcohol in parks, and Council approved the amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Reinvestment Partners (902 N. Mangum St. Food Hub)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD's Grace DeShaniel presented a performance-based Neighborhood Revitalization Grant incentive of up to $100,000 to renovate 902 N. Mangum Street into a 4,500-square-foot community food hub with shared kitchen, cold storage, and nonprofit offices. No public speakers objected and Council approved 7-0.

agenda_items.title: New Hope Church Transportation Special Use Permit (T1400001) and Major Site Plan (D1300344)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In a quasi-judicial hearing, Council heard sworn testimony from Planning/Transportation staff and church attorney Jay Ferguson on New Hope Church's 27,034 sq ft sanctuary expansion (1,576 seats, 961 Sunday peak trips), questioning a 210-ft sidewalk gap and hearing acoustical consultant Noral Stewart detail sound encapsulation measures for neighbors across the American Tobacco Trail. Council approved the TSUP, TSUP order, and major site plan 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Item: CIP Ordinance Amendment — Riverside on the Eno Failed Development Reimbursement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works' Robert Joyner explained that $74,985 in forfeited developer securities will reimburse a new developer to complete Riverside on the Eno stormwater facilities at zero cost to city taxpayers.

agenda_items.title: FY 2014–15 Budget and FY 2015–2020 CIP Adoption (Solid Waste Fee Repeal Severed)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council severed Item 10D and debated the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee at length before voting 4-3 on Steve Schewel's substitute Option 1 motion to repeal the fee in favor of property taxes (Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden voting no). Following comments from Victoria Peterson, Rafiq Zaidi, and Triangle Regional Film Commission's Rob Schoffer, Council adopted the remaining budget ordinances 6-1, with Eugene Brown voting no because the total budget incorporated the fee repeal.

agenda_items.title: Concealed Handguns at City Recreational Facilities (City Code Section 46-22 Amendment & Repeal of 46-23 to 46-27)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Patrick Baker explained that updates to Durham's code were strictly required to conform to N.C. General Assembly legislation limiting municipal authority to ban concealed carry in city parks outside specific buildings and playgrounds. After Victoria Peterson questioned the rules, Council approved the amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Review & 60-Day Timeline Report on HRC and CPRB Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield read his memorandum establishing a 60-day team review of all 44 HRC and CPRB recommendations targeting an August 21 report. Twelve public speakers—including FADE, People's Alliance, FOP, National Latino Peace Officers Association, and Hispanic business owners—divided between demanding systemic action on racial profiling and defending Chief Jose Lopez, after which Council voted 7-0 to accept the manager's report.

votes.item_title: Addition of City Manager's Priority Items (Item 33 Order, Supplemental Item 36, and HRC/CPRB Memo)
votes.notes: Reordered Item 33 after Item 32, added Item 36 (Riverside on the Eno), and added HRC/CPRB timeline memo.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested three priority adjustments to the agenda: moving Item 33 (New Hope Church major site plan) after Item 32 (New Hope Church TSUP), adding supplemental Item 36 (Riverside on the Eno CIP ordinance amendment), and placing his review and timeline memorandum regarding the Human Relations Commission and Civilian Police Review Board recommendations on the public record. Mayor Bell clarified the memo item would be open for limited public comment later in the meeting rather than a formal public hearing. Council approved the priority items 7-0.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (excluding pulled Items 10 and 11)
votes.notes: Item 10 (FY15 Budget/CIP) and Item 11 (Concealed handguns ordinance) were pulled for separate discussion.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read the consent agenda items, spanning appointments to seven boards and commissions, transportation grant ordinances, workforce investment contracts, Downtown Durham MSD and DDI agreements, the City Hall/Annex envelope CMAR contract with Balfour Beatty, Carver Street and 2014 street repairs, Fayetteville Street Elementary Safe Routes to School, the Southeast Pressure Zone elevated water storage tank, and Jordan Lake Partnership work. Items 10 and 11 were pulled from consent. The remaining consent docket was moved, seconded, and passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 35: Amendment to City Code Section 38-21 (Alcoholic Beverages in Public Buildings and Parks)
votes.notes: Clarifies permit-required alcohol consumption on the lawn of the McCown-Mangum House at Eno Park.
votes.discussion_detail: City Attorney Patrick Baker presented an amendment to Section 38-21 clarifying where permitted alcoholic beverages may be consumed on the lawn of the McCown-Mangum House at Eno Park, aligning it with existing rules for other city park buildings and emphasizing that a permit is still required. Public speaker Victoria Peterson urged caution, arguing alcohol contributes to violent crimes and underage drinking. With no further council discussion, the Council approved the ordinance amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Reinvestment Partners ($100,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant)
votes.notes: Performance-based grant up to $100,000 for 902 N. Mangum St. food hub renovation in East Geer corridor.
votes.discussion_detail: Grace DeShaniel of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented a performance-based Neighborhood Revitalization Grant incentive of up to $100,000 for nonprofit Reinvestment Partners to renovate a 4,500-square-foot building at 902 North Mangum Street outside the downtown tier into a community food hub with shared commercial kitchen, cold storage, and nonprofit offices. No incentive funds are paid until project terms are met. With no council objections and no public speakers during the hearing, Council approved the agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: New Hope Church Transportation Special Use Permit (T1400001) — Approval with Conditions
votes.notes: Quasi-judicial hearing; subject to Transportation Management Plan mitigation conditions (traffic control officer and internal lot personnel).
votes.discussion_detail: In a quasi-judicial hearing with sworn witnesses and admitted Traffic Impact Analysis and Transportation Management Plan exhibits, Planning's Jacob Wiggins and Transportation's Bill Judge presented New Hope Church's TSUP request for a 750-seat expansion (1,576 total seats generating 961 Sunday peak-hour trips) at 7619 Fayetteville Road. Council Member Diane Catotti questioned a 210-foot sidewalk gap along the north parcel frontage, and church attorney Jay Ferguson and Planner Steve Medlin confirmed the sidewalk will be extended when future expansion reaches that residential parcel. No opponents testified, and Council voted 7-0 to approve the permit with staff's recommended conditions.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Adoption of Drafted Quasi-Judicial Order for New Hope Church TSUP (T1400001)
votes.notes: Formal written order required for quasi-judicial TSUP approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after voting to approve the New Hope Church Transportation Special Use Permit, staff reminded Council that a separate motion was required to adopt the formal written order as drafted by staff. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 33: Major Site Plan — New Hope Church Building and Parking Addition (D1300344)
votes.notes: 27,034 sq ft addition and parking on 35.3 acres on Fayetteville Rd in Falls/Jordan Lake watershed.
votes.discussion_detail: Planner Steve Medlin presented D1300344 for a 27,034-square-foot addition and parking expansion at New Hope Church, noting it met all UDO standards and Board of Adjustment conditions. Council Members Steve Schewel and Diane Catotti sought assurances that the larger sanctuary would resolve prior noise complaints from neighbors across the American Tobacco Trail; acoustical consultant Noral Stewart explained the sanctuary would be encapsulated by surrounding offices, corridors, a three-layer gypsum ceiling, and a six-foot higher perimeter roof barrier, and attorney Jay Ferguson noted neighbors' counsel had reviewed the plans and supported them at the Board of Adjustment. Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden praised the church's youth outreach, and Council approved the site plan 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 36 (Supplemental): CIP Ordinance Amendment — Riverside on the Eno Failed Development Reimbursement ($74,985)
votes.notes: Uses collected developer securities ($74,985) rather than city tax dollars to complete stormwater facilities.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works' Robert Joyner presented the supplemental CIP ordinance amendment to allocate $74,985 in remaining developer securities collected between 2009 and 2011 for Riverside on the Eno so a new developer can finish the subdivision's stormwater facilities with zero city taxpayer funds. Council Members Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt thanked staff for moving the item quickly and saving city money. The ordinance amendment passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 10D (Severed): Substitute Motion Option 1 — Repeal $1.80/Month Solid Waste Fee & Adopt Commercial/Yard Waste Fee Schedules
votes.notes: Replaced the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee (~$1.4M) with equivalent property tax revenue while adjusting commercial tipping ($44/ton) and yard waste ($6/month) fees.
votes.discussion_detail: At Mayor Bell's request, Item 10D was severed from the FY 2014-15 budget for an intense policy debate. Council Member Steve Schewel moved Option 1 to repeal the $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste collection fee and replace its ~$1.4 million revenue with property taxes, joined by Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt, who argued the flat fee was regressive (hurting homeowners below ~$370,000 and renters who pay $0 directly under property tax) and would require a 56% hike next year to cover an $800,000 projected shortfall. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, Mayor Bill Bell, and Council Member Eugene Brown opposed repeal, arguing the solid waste enterprise fund already received $9.6 million in property tax subsidies, user fees akin to DATA bus fares were sound business practice, low-income residents had not complained, and adding ~0.6 cents to the tax rate risked giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate in North Carolina. The substitute motion passed 4-3, with Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 10 (Remaining Ordinances): Adoption of FY 2014–15 Budget and FY 2015–2020 Capital Improvement Plan
votes.notes: Electronic tally initially showed 7-0 at 02:07:19, but Eugene Brown immediately clarified on the record that he was voting NO on the overall budget because it included the solid waste fee repeal; Cora Cole-McFadden confirmed her Aye vote on the remaining ordinances while preserving her Nay on 10D.
votes.discussion_detail: Before voting on the remaining FY 2014-15 budget ordinances, Council heard public comments from Victoria Peterson (urging alternatives to the $94 million public safety budget), Rafiq Zaidi (demanding accountability on federal JAG informant funds), and Triangle Regional Film Commission's Rob Schoffer (requesting restoration of a $10,000 city grant). City Manager Bonfield offered to review film commission funding after recess, and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden confirmed she supported the remaining ordinances while keeping her 'no' vote on the solid waste fee repeal. Although the electronic board initially registered 7-0, Council Member Eugene Brown immediately stated on the record that he was voting against the total budget (6-1) because it incorporated the rescission of the solid waste fee.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Pulled from Consent): Amendment to City Code Section 46-22 and Repeal of Sections 46-23 to 46-27 (Concealed Carry in Parks)
votes.notes: Conforms Durham City Code to N.C. General Assembly preemption on concealed handguns in municipal parks.
votes.discussion_detail: Speaker Victoria Peterson pulled Item 11 to ask City Attorney Patrick Baker whether residents would still be allowed to carry concealed handguns in parks and asked for county jail detention statistics for Durham Police arrests. Baker referred jail counts to the Sheriff's Office and explained that the ordinance update did not originate locally—rather, 2012-2013 state legislation restricted cities from prohibiting concealed weapons in parks outside specific buildings and playground structures, requiring Durham to conform its code to state law. Council approved the amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Acceptance of City Manager's Review Plan and 60-Day Timeline on HRC and CPRB Recommendations
votes.notes: Sets ~60-day review period targeting the August 21 work session for response to all 44 HRC and CPRB recommendations.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield read his memorandum outlining a 60-day team review of the 34 HRC recommendations and 10 CPRB recommendations—consulting DPD, the City Attorney, peer cities, and advocacy groups—with a final report targeted for August 21. Twelve public speakers addressed the item: advocates (including Chris Tiffany, Rafiq Zaidi, Nancy Wilson, David Hall, Victoria Peterson, and Charlie Reese) urged immediate action on written vehicle search consent, complaint handling, and systemic racial disparities, while Hispanic business owners and FOP representative Hilton Cancel defended Chief Jose Lopez against calls for his removal. After Eugene Brown voiced support for the manager's letter, Council voted 7-0 to accept the report.

disagreements.issue: Repeal of the $1.80/Month Solid Waste Collection Fee vs. Property Tax Replacement (Item 10D & Final Budget)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 on repealing the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replacing its $1.4 million revenue with property taxes, leading Eugene Brown to vote no (6-1) on the final overall budget.
disagreements.side_a_position: Repeal the flat $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste fee and fund the $1.4 million through the property tax rate.
side_a_arguments: A flat per-household fee is regressive, charging a $75,000 homeowner or low-income renter the same $21.60/year as a $500,000 homeowner.
Any homeowner below ~$370,000 in assessed value—and single-family/duplex renters who pay $0 directly under property tax—pays less under Option 1.
Keeping the fee would require a 56% fee hike next year to cover a projected $800,000 solid waste shortfall.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain the $1.80/month solid waste user fee to stabilize the solid waste enterprise fund and avoid raising property taxes.
side_b_arguments: The $20 million solid waste fund already receives $9.6 million in general-fund property tax subsidies from all property owners, including businesses and multi-family residents without city pickup.
Like DATA bus fares, a modest $1.80/month user fee for households receiving collection service is not regressive, and DSS assistance covers hardship cases.
Replacing the fee plus county/other increases risks giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate among North Carolina's largest cities, hurting competitiveness.
disagreements.resolution: Option 1 repeal passed 4-3; the remaining FY 2014-15 budget ordinances then passed 6-1 with Eugene Brown dissenting because the final budget incorporated the fee repeal.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 2, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Diane Catotti absent, the Durham City Council rejected a resolution approving recommendations of the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) on a 3-3 tie vote after Steve Schewel objected to proposals such as closing Dillard Street, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the TSS report. Council held its FY 2014-15 budget e-town hall and public hearing—receiving comments on broken sidewalks, Stonehill Estates street paving, and repealing the solid waste fee—and unanimously approved (6-0) the 2013 Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Assessment Report, two street closings, the consent agenda (including receiving HRC racial profiling recommendations), and a resolution memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou.

agenda_items.title: Recognitions, Excused Absences for July 24 Work Session, and Addition of Dr. Maya Angelou Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Eddie Davis honored pioneers Hortense McClinton and Kelly Bryant, Council voted 6-0 to excuse Davis and Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden from the July 24 work session, and added supplemental Item 35 (resolution memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou) 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously adopted the consent agenda 6-0, including minutes, street acceptances, Phillips impact fee appeal, dedicated funding and grants audits, Ninth Street infrastructure agreement amendment, East End Connector right-of-way conveyance, FY15 benefits recommendations, four board/commission annual reports, Windmere Ridge reimbursement, telephone system improvement, Lanier Parking amendment, Erwin Rd lighting, water/wastewater contracts, and receiving the HRC recommendations on DPD racial profiling.

agenda_items.title: Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dan Jewell of Durham Area Designers urged Council to ensure TSS scenarios were treated strictly as conceptual and subject to project-specific studies and renewed public engagement. Council Member Steve Schewel opposed accepting the study's recommendations—citing the proposed closing of Dillard Street—and the approval resolution failed on a 3-3 tie before Schewel's motion merely to receive the report passed 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Approval resolution failed 3-3; Motion to receive report passed 6-0 (Catotti absent)

agenda_items.title: FY 2014–15 Proposed Budget E-Town Hall and Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: WRAL's Ken Smith moderated an interactive e-town hall with Council answering resident questions on sidewalk funding ($100,000 repair budget), potholes/state vs. city streets, bike lanes, public safety, solid waste cuts, the half-cent parks maintenance tax, Long Meadow Pool's electrical safety closure, historic district staffing, the Mayor's poverty initiative, and youth employment. During the public hearing, speakers urged repealing the solid waste fee, paving Stonehill Estates, doubling sidewalk repair funding, and opposing tax hikes before Council closed the hearing and accepted comments 6-0.

agenda_items.title: 2013 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) of the Durham Comprehensive Plan (A1400002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Aaron Cain presented the 2013 Comprehensive Plan EAR consisting of 54 edited or new policies and three county parcel future land use technical changes (endorsed 12-0 by the Planning Commission and adopted May 27 by County Commissioners). With no public speakers, Council adopted the EAR 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Street Closings: Unnamed Alley off Alley #12 (SC1400005) and Chaparro Drive (SC1300005)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Pat Young presented two street closings: a 50-linear-foot portion of an unnamed alley east of Buchanan Blvd (requested by Julianne Darby, who explained why neighbors' garage access prevented closing the entire alley) and a 1,090-linear-foot portion of Chaparro Drive near Southpoint Mall requested by Hendrick Automotive Group. Both passed 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously adopted a supplemental resolution honoring the life and achievements of Dr. Maya Angelou, with Mayor Bell noting a memorial program at Wake Forest University.

votes.item_title: Procedural Motion: Excuse Absence of Council Member Eddie Davis from July 24 Work Session
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Following his remarks recognizing Hortense McClinton and Kelly Bryant, Council Member Eddie Davis requested an excused absence for the July 24, 2014 work session. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved 6-0 with Diane Catotti absent.

votes.item_title: Procedural Motion: Excuse Absence of Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden from July 24 Work Session
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. Cole-McFadden noted she would be attending a national committee meeting in St. Paul, Minnesota on city business.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden requested an excused absence for the July 24, 2014 work session to attend a national committee meeting in St. Paul, Minnesota on city business. Council approved the excused absence 6-0 with Diane Catotti absent.

votes.item_title: Addition of City Clerk's Supplemental Item 35 (Resolution Memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou)
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: City Clerk D. Ann Gray requested adding supplemental Item 35, a resolution memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou, to the June 2 agenda. Council voted 6-0 to add the resolution, and Mayor Bell noted copies were on members' desks and asked staff to check on delivering it for a memorial program at Wake Forest University.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Resolution Approving Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Recommendations
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. Electronic roll call failed on a 3-3 tie; Steve Schewel explicitly spoke and voted Nay while the remaining 5 present members (Bell, Cole-McFadden, Brown, Davis, Moffitt) split 3-2 without individual votes read aloud.
votes.discussion_detail: Dan Jewell, president of Durham Area Designers (DAD), addressed Item 28, urging Council to emphasize that the Durham Traffic Separation Study's limited scenarios were conceptual rather than recommended solutions and warning that some proposals could harm city livability unless subjected to immediate project-specific studies and public engagement. Council Member Steve Schewel argued against adopting the resolution—even with caveats—because accepting recommendations such as closing Dillard Street creates public expectations that those closures are settled policy, urging Council to merely receive the report instead. The motion to approve the resolution failed on a 3-3 tie vote with Diane Catotti absent.

votes.item_title: Item 28 (Subsequent Motion): Motion to Receive the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Report
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. Adopted after the resolution to approve TSS recommendations failed 3-3.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after the resolution approving the Durham Traffic Separation Study recommendations failed on a 3-3 tie, Council Member Steve Schewel moved that the Council simply receive the TSS report without endorsing its specific street closure recommendations. The motion was seconded and passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Acceptance of Public Hearing Comments on Proposed FY 2014–15 City Budget
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. ASR transcript misheard '6-0' as 'six to six' at 01:54:28.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the 60-minute e-town hall moderated by WRAL's Ken Smith, nine residents spoke during the formal budget public hearing: Charlie Reese (Durham People's Alliance) urged repealing the $1.80/month solid waste fee; Stephen Hopkins, Peter Skillern (Reinvestment Partners), former Council Member Larissa Sabol, and Kevin Armstrong called for doubling the $100,000 sidewalk repair budget and prioritizing ADA/redevelopment corridors; Gwen Silver and James O. Williams demanded city paving for Stonehill Estates' failed subdivision streets; Donald Bryson (Americans for Prosperity) opposed property tax increases; and Victoria Peterson advocated paid youth job-training stipends. Council members thanked residents and staff, and Mayor Bell noted the final budget vote was slated for June 16 before Council voted 6-0 to receive the comments.

votes.item_title: Item 30: 2013 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) of the Durham Comprehensive Plan (A1400002)
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. ASR misheard '6-0' as 'six is the one' at 01:57:16. Adopts 54 policy updates and 3 county parcel FLUM technical changes.
votes.discussion_detail: Planner Aaron Cain presented Case A1400002, the 2013 Evaluation and Assessment Report of the Durham Comprehensive Plan, covering 54 edited or new policy statements and three county parcel future land use map technical updates reflecting acquired agricultural and open-space easements (with zero BOCC FLUM amendments requiring rectification). The Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 and the Board of County Commissioners adopted the EAR on May 27, 2014. With no public speakers, Council voted 6-0 to approve.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Street Closing — Unnamed Alley Perpendicular to Alley #12 (SC1400005)
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. Closes 50-linear-foot terminal portion of alley east of Buchanan Blvd and south of Urban Ave.
votes.discussion_detail: Planner Pat Young presented SC1400005, a request by Julianne Darby to close a 50-linear-foot terminal segment of an unnamed alley off Alley #12 near Buchanan Boulevard and Urban Avenue, noting no adverse agency impacts. Responding to Council Member Don Moffitt's question about why the entire short alley was not closed, Young and applicant Julianne Darby (705 Watts St.) explained that four neighboring homes south of her had paved and maintained the remaining two-thirds for garage access and closing it would cut off their garages. Moffitt moved approval, seconded, passing 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Street Closing — Chaparro Drive (SC1300005)
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting. Closes 1,090 linear feet west of Fayetteville Rd and south of Renaissance Pkwy for Hendrick Automotive Group.
votes.discussion_detail: Planner Pat Young presented SC1300005, an application by Hendrick Automotive Group to close a 1,090-linear-foot portion of Chaparro Drive adjacent to Southpoint Mall to facilitate automotive sales development. City, county, and utility reviewers identified no adverse impacts, and no public speakers appeared. Council closed the public hearing and approved the street closing 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 35 (Supplemental): Resolution Memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou
votes.notes: Diane Catotti absent from meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: As the final agenda action, Council took up supplemental Item 35, the resolution memorializing Dr. Maya Angelou. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 6-0 with Diane Catotti absent.

disagreements.issue: Acceptance vs. Mere Receipt of the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Recommendations (Item 28)
disagreements.summary: Council tied 3-3 on adopting a resolution accepting the Durham Traffic Separation Study recommendations, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the report without endorsing its conceptual street closures.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the staff-recommended resolution accepting the TSS report with caveats requiring future project-specific studies and public input.
side_a_arguments: The resolution explicitly conditioned any implementation on subsequent project-specific studies, public engagement, and City Council approval.
Accepting the final report concluded the study phase while preserving Council veto power over individual rail crossings.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the approval resolution and merely receive the report so conceptual closures like Dillard Street are not treated as adopted city policy.
side_b_arguments: Accepting recommendations lacking broad community support creates an expectation that projects like closing Dillard Street are moving forward.
Durham Area Designers noted the limited scenarios evaluated were conceptual at best and potentially damaging to downtown livability.
disagreements.resolution: The resolution accepting the TSS recommendations failed on a 3-3 tie (Diane Catotti absent), and Steve Schewel's motion merely to receive the report passed 6-0.

meetings.title: Proposed Budget for Fiscal Year 2014-2015 for City of Durham, North Carolina
meetings.executive_summary: This video captures City Manager Tom Bonfield's formal presentation of the proposed $386.7 million Fiscal Year 2014-2015 City of Durham budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan to Mayor Bill Bell and the City Council. The proposal featured a 1.29-cent property tax rate increase to 58.04 cents per $100 of assessed value to cover voter-approved debt service and absorb 16 police officer and 15 firefighter positions from expiring grants, alongside a return to differentiated pay-for-performance raises (averaging 3% for general employees and 3.5% for police and fire), a 7.5% stormwater rate increase, 3% water and sewer rate increases, and $1 million for street repaving. Mayor Bell noted that Council budget workshops would begin on Wednesday, May 28, ahead of a June 2 E-Town Hall.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Fiscal Year 2014-2015 Budget and Fiscal Year 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented the proposed FY 2014-2015 total budget of $386.7 million (up 2.7%) and general fund budget of $173.6 million (up 2.3%), recommending a 1.29-cent property tax increase (0.73 cents for voter-approved debt service and 0.56 cents for 31 previously grant-funded police and fire positions) while maintaining a 13.5% general fund balance reserve. The plan proposed returning to differentiated pay-for-performance increases averaging 3% for general staff and 3.5% for public safety, funding $93 million in capital improvement projects, increasing street repaving to $1 million, adding $400,000 for sidewalks, raising water/sewer rates 3% and stormwater rates 7.5%, and presenting a potential additional half-cent tax option for parks maintenance during upcoming workshops. Bonfield also highlighted fiber broadband readiness, Southside revitalization (132 rental units nearing completion and 19 of 48 home lots reserved), a $96,000 HUD fair housing grant, and a $9.6 million general fund subsidy to the solid waste fund.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members convened on May 19, 2014, opening with recognitions for National Public Works Week and a briefing from Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson on emergency recovery from a confirmed EF1 tornado the prior weekend. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (excluding Item 2), heard City Manager Tom Bonfield's formal presentation of the proposed $386.7 million FY 2014-2015 budget, and approved a 7.5% stormwater rate increase, the 123.5-acre Corners at Brier Creek consolidated annexation and initial zoning, and a Rougemont watershed text amendment. Council also referred a tree-coverage UDO text amendment back to staff and approved a Google Fiber network hut license agreement 7-0 after public comment urging local hiring.

agenda_items.title: Recognitions, National Public Works Week Proclamation, and Tornado Recovery Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell recognized Cubmaster Emeritus Masony Brooks for 43 years with Pack 137 at St. Joseph AME Church and proclaimed National Public Works Week for Director Marvin Williams and department staff. At Councilmember Don Moffitt's request, Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson briefed Council on the multi-agency response to an EF1 tornado and torrential rain the prior Thursday night, noting debris clearing by Public Works, General Services, Solid Waste, Parks and Recreation, the Sheriff's Office, Red Cross, and Baptist Men's Association. Councilmember Eddie Davis and Moffitt also praised Parks and Recreation staff for hosting the Bimbe Festival at Rock Quarry Park.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Minutes, Southside HOME Funds, Compensation Plan, Water/Sewer Rates & Capital Projects)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda with the exception of Item 2 (Network Hut License Agreement with Google), which was pulled by resident Victoria Peterson. Approved items included council minutes, a $500,000 HOME Investment Partnerships amendment with Southside Revitalization Phase 1 LP, renewal of the Urban Search and Rescue MOA, compensation and classification plan recommendations, FY 2014-2015 water and sewer rates (averaging 3% increase), water and sewer capital facilities fee updates, water/sewer master plan engineering contract amendment #2, and the Turnage Heights lift station abandonment project.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY 2014-2015 Budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented the proposed $386.7 million total budget ($173.6 million general fund) for FY 2014-2015, proposing a 1.29-cent property tax increase to 58.04 cents per $100 assessed value to fund voter-approved debt service and 31 police and fire positions previously supported by expired grants. The budget restored differentiated pay-for-performance raises (3% general, 3.5% police/fire), increased street repaving to $1 million, budgeted $400,000 for sidewalks, and outlined a potential half-cent tax option for parks maintenance at upcoming workshops starting May 28. During public comment, Victoria Peterson praised fiber initiatives but urged addressing violent crime, arrests, and indigent defense delays in the Durham County Jail.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment – Tree Coverage Calculations (TC13-00002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young of the Planning Department reported that TC13-00002 regarding tree coverage calculations was first heard February 3 and continued to May 19, and that the applicant had recently requested referral back to the administration to make modifications. Staff recommended closing the public hearing and referring the item back to the administration to be re-advertised at the applicant's cost. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – The Corners at Brier Creek Initial Zoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation petition, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for approximately 123.5 acres at the northern corner of T.W. Alexander Drive and US Highway 70, permitting up to 141 single-family homes or a place of worship with adequate utility capacity and revenue-positive fiscal impact. Attorney Patrick Byker and engineer Tommy Craven represented the development team, and staff noted a scrivener's error in Attachment 11 correcting the hearing date to May 19. Following the 7-0 vote, Mayor Bell and Byker discussed a 1.07-acre boundary overlap in Raleigh's jurisdiction resulting from the T.W. Alexander extension that might require a local legislative act if not resolved administratively.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment – Watershed Protection Overlay, Rural Village (TC13-00003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a text amendment to Article 8 of the UDO modifying lot size and impervious surface limits within the Rougemont Rural Village, which lies entirely within Durham County jurisdiction. The amendment was brought to maintain consistency between the county and city versions of the UDO after the Board of County Commissioners adopted it unanimously and the Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 on February 11, 2014. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Adoption of Proposed Stormwater Rates for FY 2015
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Paul Wiebke of Public Works presented a proposed 7.5% stormwater rate increase effective July 1, 2014, to fund stormwater retrofit capital projects required under Falls Lake Stage 1 existing development rules and NPDES permit compliance. Wiebke noted the 7.5% increase was 1% lower than projected the prior year and would raise annual bills by $2.76 (Tier 1), $5.64 (Tier 2), and $11.28 (Tier 3) for residential customers and roughly $110 for non-residential customers. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Network Hut License Agreement between the City of Durham and Google
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Consent Item 2, welcoming Google Fiber to Durham while raising concerns that city property sites were not yet specified and urging the city to ensure local hiring—including for more than 200 locally trained copper and fiber workers who often face employment barriers due to criminal records. Mayor Bell responded that while the fiber deployments with Google and AT&T were still in early stages, the city would place strong emphasis on employing local residents if the projects proceed.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, excluding pulled Item 2)
votes.notes: Item 2 (Google Network Hut License Agreement) was pulled by public speaker Victoria Peterson for separate consideration.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read through the consent agenda headings, covering approval of minutes (Item 1), a $500,000 HOME Investment Partnerships amendment for Southside Revitalization Phase 1 LP (Item 4), renewal of the Urban Search and Rescue MOA (Item 5), compensation and classification plan recommendations (Item 6), FY 2014-2015 water and sewer rates averaging a 3% increase (Item 7), water and sewer capital facilities fee updates (Item 8), a water/sewer master plan engineering contract amendment (Item 9), and the Turnage Heights lift station abandonment project (Item 10). Public speaker Victoria Peterson pulled Item 2 for separate discussion later in the meeting. With no council questions on the remaining items, Council moved, seconded, and approved the consent agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12: UDO Text Amendment – Tree Coverage Calculations (TC13-00002) Referral Back to Administration
votes.notes: Closed public hearing and referred text amendment back to administration at applicant's request, to be re-advertised at applicant's cost.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young certified statutory public notice and explained that TC13-00002 regarding tree coverage calculations had first been heard on February 3 and continued to May 19. The applicant subsequently requested that the item be referred back to the administration to make modifications in coordination with staff, with re-notification costs borne by the applicant. Mayor Bell opened the public hearing, noted no council questions and no public speakers, closed the hearing, and entertained a motion to accept the staff recommendation. Council voted 7-0 to refer the text amendment back to the administration.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension Agreement, and Initial Zoning – The Corners at Brier Creek
votes.notes: Approves utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial RR zoning for ~123.5 acres at T.W. Alexander Dr & US 70.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented the consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation petition, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for 123.5 acres at T.W. Alexander Drive and US Highway 70, reporting adequate water/sewer capacity and a positive fiscal impact analysis for up to 141 single-family homes or a place of worship, while noting the applicant anticipated seeking higher-density rezoning later. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and engineer Tommy Craven appeared in support, and staff noted for the record a scrivener's correction changing the order date from the 18th to the 19th. With no public opposition, Councilmember Don Moffitt moved approval and Council passed the item 7-0. After the vote, Mayor Bell and Byker discussed a 1.07-acre sliver lying within Raleigh's jurisdiction due to the T.W. Alexander road extension, noting it could require a local legislative act by the Durham delegation if Raleigh and Durham planners could not resolve it administratively.

votes.item_title: Item 14: UDO Text Amendment – Watershed Protection Overlay, Rural Village (TC13-00003)
votes.notes: Matches county-adopted UDO Article 8 standards for Rougemont Rural Village.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented TC13-00003, amending Article 8 of the Unified Development Ordinance regarding lot size and impervious surface limitations in the Rougemont Rural Village. Because Rougemont lies entirely within Durham County's jurisdiction, there was no direct impact inside city limits, and the amendment was needed solely to keep the city and county versions of the joint UDO consistent after unanimous County approval and a 12-0 Planning Commission recommendation on February 11, 2014. No council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and approved the text amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Adoption of Proposed Stormwater Rates for FY 2015 (7.5% Increase)
votes.notes: Effective July 1, 2014; funds Falls Lake Stage 1 stormwater retrofits and NPDES compliance.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works representative Paul Wiebke presented the proposed 7.5% stormwater rate increase effective July 1, 2014, explaining that it funds repair, operation, and maintenance of city stormwater systems as well as capital retrofits mandated by Falls Lake watershed rules and the city's NPDES permit. Wiebke noted current rates sit near the middle of benchmark peer cities and that the 7.5% increase was 1% lower than projected the previous year, translating to annual increases of $2.76 for Tier 1, $5.64 for Tier 2, $11.28 for Tier 3 residential customers, and roughly $110 for non-residential accounts. No council questions or public comments were offered during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and adopted the rate increase 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 2 (Pulled Consent): Network Hut License Agreement between City of Durham and Google
votes.notes: Pulled by Victoria Peterson to raise local hiring and reentry employment concerns.
votes.discussion_detail: Resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 2 from the consent agenda to ask how many homes Google Fiber would serve, which city properties would host fiber huts, and how the city would ensure Durham residents—particularly low-income residents and over 200 individuals previously trained locally in copper and fiber cabling who face hiring barriers due to felony records—receive installation jobs rather than being bypassed. Mayor Bell replied that the city could not yet answer all project specifics, as both Google and AT&T were still evaluating proposals, but assured Peterson that if fiber projects requiring city support move forward, the city would place strong emphasis on employing local residents. Council then moved, seconded, and approved the Google network hut license agreement 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 5, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on May 5, 2014, adopting the consent agenda and holding public hearings on the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for federal HUD and local dedicated housing funds, prior-year HUD grant reconciliations, inspections permit fee updates, the UDI Farm comprehensive plan amendment and RS-20 rezoning (approved 6-0 with Mayor Bell recused due to his employment at UDI CDC), and a street closing adjacent to Lakewood Elementary School. Council also heard extensive testimony from Housing for New Hope clients, Urban Ministries, Durham Community Land Trustees, and the Citizens Advisory Committee during the Annual Action Plan hearing, and reviewed the Durham Police Department's Q1 2014 crime report showing a 36% spike in Part 1 violent crime driven by multi-victim shootings alongside the launch of a juvenile misdemeanor diversion program.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Council Comments, and City Manager Priority Agenda Adjustments

City Manager Tom Bonfield requested holding Consent Item 7 (CASA HOME funds) until after Item 26 and adding Supplemental Item 31 (Q1 Public Safety Report), while Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden flagged a follow-up question on Item 6 regarding how Connecting Youth verifies participants are Durham County residents.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for CDBG, HOME, and ESG Funds

Councilmembers Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel questioned $192,000 in gap financing for Vermillion while praising a shift raising Habitat for Humanity second-mortgage assistance in Northeast Central Durham from $120,000 to $180,000; Council voted 7-0 to receive comments and then 7-0 to adopt the plan.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City-County Inspections Permit Fee Ordinance

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 21, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on April 21, 2014, approving the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 7), extending an incentive deadline for The Gentian Group's Hotel Durham project, and voting 6-1—over Mayor Bell's dissent—to approve a $3.97 million, 15-year economic development incentive agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East for the 26-story City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment. Bell argued the contract should guarantee a minimum annual property tax yield of $327,400, while the council majority and legal/finance staff warned that tying payments directly to tax yields risked violating state constitutional prohibitions on tax rebates and could jeopardize project financing. Council also unanimously approved targeted revisions to the Economic Development Policy enabling Ninth Street corridor grants after Schewel and Bell flagged broader policy reforms for a future city-county overhaul, approved the pulled MCNC telecommunications license agreement 7-0, and excused two work-session absences.

agenda_items.title: Earth Day, Mayor's Water Conservation Challenge, and National Community Development Week Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented proclamations for Earth Day (accepted by Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker), the Wyland Foundation National Mayor's Challenge for Water Conservation (with Water Management Assistant Director Vicki Westbrook noting Durham ranked 9th nationally among peer cities), and National Community Development Week marking 40 years of CDBG and 24 years of HOME programs (accepted by Reginald Johnson). Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden also recognized Carolina Theatre staff attending ahead of their consent agenda services agreement.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (DCLT Southside Funds, Carolina Theatre Agreement, TIGER Grant, Sidewalks & Infrastructure)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda with the exception of Item 7 (MCNC telecommunications license agreement), which was pulled by Victoria Peterson. Approved items included minutes, a Workforce Development Board appointment, dedicated housing and HOME funds for Durham Community Land Trustees in Southside, a partial payment to Parkwood Volunteer Fire Department, an 800 MHz radio agreement with Fayetteville, the Carolina Theatre building and services agreement, CFP development reimbursement amendments, a sidewalk grant agreement on Campus Walk Avenue and LaSalle Street, BPAC and Recreation Advisory Commission annual reports, sewer pipe/manhole rehabilitation contract SR-58, and a FY 2014 TIGER planning grant application.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to Economic Incentive Contract with The Gentian Group LLC (Hotel Durham / Holland Hotel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Thomas Leathers of OEWD presented an amendment extending Section 3.1.1's deadline to secure a final certificate of compliance to November 30 following delays caused by earlier right-of-way and easement public hearings. Councilmember Steve Schewel sought clarification on the $400,000 inspections certificate figure, and Leathers confirmed it reflected good-faith expenditures already made by the developer and created no additional city liability until the project is completed. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East, LLC (City Center & Jack Tar)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Kevin Dick, developer Greg Hills, and HITT Contracting's Amanda Moreau presented the $85 million ($65 million qualified capital investment) redevelopment featuring a 26-story mixed-use tower at 119 W. Parrish St., restoration of five historic facades on Parrish and Main Streets, and renovation of the Jack Tar Motel and 260-space parking deck at 202 N. Corcoran St., backed by up to $3.97 million in city incentives over 15 years and 15% Durham-based / 5% SDBE contracting goals. Downtown Durham Inc., DCVB, the Chamber, the Institute of Minority Economic Development, and Pizzeria Toro spoke in support, while Council questioned facade bracing, Duke office relocation vs. new jobs, financing via a Virginia REIT, condo vs. rental flexibility, and construction disruption. Mayor Bell opposed approving the contract without language guaranteeing at least $327,400 in annual general fund property taxes across future revaluations and asked to hold the vote until Thursday, but the council majority called the question and approved the agreement 6-1.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Revisions to Economic Development Incentive Policy (Ninth Street Corridor & Grant Updates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reginald Jones of OEWD presented targeted updates adding the Ninth Street commercial corridor as an incentive target area beyond the CDA, setting a $50,000 private investment floor for non-downtown CDA building grants, merging sign/facade grants into retail/professional services grants up to $20,000, extending completion timelines from 12 to 18 months, and renaming the urban growth area. Victoria Peterson urged greater African American downtown property ownership and African sister-city ties (Mayor Bell noted Arusha, Tanzania). Steve Schewel and Mayor Bell raised broad policy reforms for the upcoming joint city-county overhaul—including lowering the 16% incentive cap, tying job incentives to Durham residents, requiring 60% AMI affordable housing bonuses, and ending non-city capital incentives—and agreed to approve the narrow Ninth Street revisions 7-0 after staff warned deferral would stall Ninth Street merchant grants.

agenda_items.title: Telecommunications License Agreement with Microelectronics Center of North Carolina (MCNC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Consent Item 7 to publicly thank MCNC for hiring Durham residents with criminal records and challenging backgrounds in past copper and fiber optic installations, urging the city to encourage other fiber providers to adopt similar second-chance hiring practices. Councilmember Steve Schewel echoed Peterson's remarks.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Thursday Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: At the close of the meeting, Council voted separately in two unanimous 7-0 votes to excuse absences from the upcoming Thursday work session, including Councilmember Eugene Brown, while Councilmember Diane Catotti noted a family reunion in Eastern Maryland.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East, LLC (City Center Tower & Jack Tar Motel)
votes.notes: Approves ~$3.97M 15-year incentive for 26-story City Center tower, facade restorations, and Jack Tar Motel/parking deck redevelopment; Mayor Bell voted No over lack of a guaranteed minimum property tax yield.
votes.discussion_detail: OEWD's Kevin Dick, developer Greg Hills, and contractor Amanda Moreau presented the City Center and Jack Tar redevelopment ($85M total / $65M qualified capital investment), featuring a 26-story tower at 119 W. Parrish St., restoration of five historic facades, and conversion of the Jack Tar Motel at 202 N. Corcoran St. into a 74-room hotel with a 260-space parking deck, supported by a 15-year incentive (~$3.9M / $265K annually) and 15% Durham-based / 5% SDBE contracting goals. Leaders from DDI, DCVB, the Chamber, IMED, and Pizzeria Toro spoke in support, while Councilmembers Davis, Brown, Schewel, and Cole-McFadden probed local business outreach, facade bracing safety, REIT financing, condo vs. rental options, and construction traffic. Mayor Bill Bell objected to Section 2.1, insisting the contract should bind the project to generate at least $327,400 per year in general fund property taxes across future revaluations rather than only measuring capital investment, and asked to hold the vote until Thursday. Finance Director David Boyd and City Attorney Fred Lamar warned that directly tying payments to tax yields or developer make-up payments risked violating North Carolina's constitutional ban on tax rebates, and the council majority called the question and approved the agreement 6-1 with Bell voting No.

votes.notes: Adds Ninth Street commercial corridor target area and merges small-business grant programs; broader policy overhaul deferred to joint city-county strategic plan.
votes.discussion_detail: OEWD's Reginald Jones presented targeted revisions to the 2011 Economic Development Policy to add the Ninth Street commercial corridor beyond the CDA, set a $50,000 minimum investment for non-downtown CDA building grants, merge sign and facade grants into retail/professional services grants up to $20,000, and extend completion deadlines from 12 to 18 months. Public speaker Victoria Peterson urged expanding African American property ownership downtown and partnering with African sister cities, to which Mayor Bell noted Arusha, Tanzania is already a Durham sister city. Councilmember Steve Schewel flagged multiple concerns for the upcoming joint city-county policy review—including lowering the 16% maximum cap, dropping parking-rate offsets, restricting non-city capital incentives, and defining affordable housing bonuses at 60% AMI—while Mayor Bell pushed to tie job incentives to Durham residents and initially proposed deferring action. After staff explained deferral would block Ninth Street merchant grants until after summer while having negligible job-incentive impact, Council approved the revisions 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7 (Pulled Consent): Telecommunications License Agreement with Microelectronics Center of North Carolina (MCNC)
votes.notes: Pulled by Victoria Peterson to commend MCNC for hiring ex-offenders.
votes.discussion_detail: Victoria Peterson pulled Item 7 from the consent agenda to publicly commend MCNC and its representative Joe for hiring Durham residents with past criminal records and challenging backgrounds during prior copper and fiber optic projects. disagreements.issue: Austin Lawrence Partners (City Center / Jack Tar) Incentive Agreement – Minimum Guaranteed Property Tax Yield vs. Capital Investment Metric
disagreements.summary: Mayor Bill Bell dissented in a 6-1 vote on the $3.97 million, 15-year incentive agreement for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, insisting the contract include an absolute minimum annual property tax yield ($327,400) rather than relying solely on capital investment thresholds, while the six council members and city finance/legal staff supported approving the agreement as drafted under existing policy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $3.97M incentive agreement immediately as drafted under existing economic development policy, relying on conservative tax assessor estimates ($60.9M assessed value) and avoiding constitutional tax-rebate risks.
side_a_arguments: Existing city policy bases incentives on qualified capital investment ($65M minimum) rather than actual tax revenue yields because directly linking incentives to tax revenues or requiring make-up payments risks violating the North Carolina Constitution's prohibition on tax rebates.

Finance staff already applied conservative buffers by basing projections on the tax assessor's $60.9M valuation (about 10% below the $65M minimum investment), capping the incentive at ~80.9% of projected property tax, and excluding ~$3.4M in projected hotel occupancy and sales taxes.
Delaying approval past April would disrupt the developer's imminent REIT financing term sheet and push back demolition and construction timelines.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold the agreement until Thursday and amend Section 2.1 (or attach Exhibit D) to guarantee that the project generates at least $327,400 annually in general fund property tax revenue regardless of future property revaluations.
side_b_arguments: While the city's 15-year payout (~$265K/year) is fixed in dollars, future countywide property revaluations typically lower tax rates and could erode actual property tax inflows below the $327,400 projection.

Future councils paying out general fund dollars over 15 years should have contractual certainty of the minimum property tax revenue returning to the general fund rather than relying on non-binding memos or uncertain sales/hotel taxes.
disagreements.resolution: Council rejected Mayor Bell's request to hold the item until Thursday and approved the incentive agreement 6-1, with Bell voting No; City Attorney Fred Lamar agreed to examine revenue-guarantee mechanisms during the upcoming comprehensive Economic Development Policy overhaul.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 7, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on April 7, 2014, presenting ceremonial recognitions including Little River Elementary fifth-grader Betty Closs (the region's first African American Duke Regional Spelling Bee champion) and a memorial resolution for civic and banking leader F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr. Council approved a modified $2,400 window-easement agreement at 112 West Main Street, adopted the consent agenda, and unanimously approved the 105-unit Chapel Creek consolidated annexation and PDR 8.00 initial zoning near NC 54. Following extensive public comment from Healing with Care advocating broader access to homelessness funding, Council unanimously approved a rapid-rehousing contract amendment with Housing for New Hope while urging greater transparency in funding outreach, and amended and adopted FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines directing staff to study up to one cent per $100 valuation for parks and trails maintenance alongside municipal tax and fee comparisons.

agenda_items.title: Recognitions for Betty Closs, F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr. Memorial, Week of the Young Child, Crime Victims' Rights, Fair Housing, and 911 Communications
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell recognized fifth-grader Betty Closs for winning the Duke Regional Spelling Bee, presented a certified copy of Resolution #987 memorializing F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr. to Dr. E. Lavonia Ingram Allison, and issued proclamations for the Week of the Young Child (Durham's Partnership for Children), National Crime Victims' Rights Week (DPD Victim Services Unit), Fair Housing Month (Human Relations Division), and National Public Safety 911 Communications Officer Week honoring Employee of the Year Shannon Carson.

agenda_items.title: City Attorney Priority Modification – Agreement for Windows at 112 West Main Street (Empress Development LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney presented a priority modification to Consent Item 12 (originally listed as an air-rights easement sale at 106 West Main Street), replacing motions A and B to authorize the City Manager to execute an agreement with Empress Development LLC granting legal rights to install windows in the east wall of 112 West Main Street in exchange for $2,400.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Minutes, Appointments, Social Media Audit, Public Art, Street Repaving, East End Connector)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda excluding pulled Items 6 and 7 and previously approved Item 12, approving minutes, DPAC and DCVB/TDA appointments, the 2013 boards and commissions attendance report, the February 2014 social media performance audit, a public art location change for Brenda Miller Holmes, a CCB Plaza sculpture donation, the January 2014 bid report, a HUD Fair Housing Grant amendment, a USGS rainfall/streamflow agreement, a 2013 street repaving contract increase, and NCDOT agreements for the U-0071 East End Connector.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – Chapel Creek (Utility Extension, BDG13-10, Initial Zoning Z13-14)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation (BDG13-10), and initial PDR 8.00 zoning (Z13-14) for 17.1 acres at George King Road and Crossland Drive north of NC 54 to allow up to 105 residential units (recommended 12-0 by the Planning Commission). Eastwood Park neighbors Lynn Scott and Chris Selby supported the eight-units-per-acre density cap, and developer representative Jared Edens proffered $13,000 ($500 per projected student) to Durham Public Schools while keeping single-family homes adjacent to existing neighbors. Councilmember Steve Schewel questioned staff on when NC 54 capacity improvements might occur through NCDOT prioritization.

agenda_items.title: Third Amendment to Contract for ESG and Dedicated Housing Fund Rapid Rehousing Services with Housing for New Hope
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden pulled Item 7 after opposing suspension of rules at the work session so the public could address equitable access to rapid-rehousing funds. Four speakers from Healing with Care (Dr. Sharon Elliott-Bynum, Darryl Hickman, Kelly Fenner, and Carolyn Hinton) described housing 42 homeless individuals including high-barrier veterans and urged competitive funding access. Community Development's Larry Jarvis clarified the contract added FY 2014 funds ($200,000 dedicated housing penny and $67,000 ESG) as an extension to Housing for New Hope—the sole applicant in the publicized FY 2015 ESG/dedicated-fund round—whereas Healing with Care had applied through the separate Continuum of Care process, and Council members urged clearer outreach and simpler application communications before approving the contract 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines – Parks Maintenance Amendment and Guidelines Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Councilmember Steve Schewel pulled Item 6 to propose a budget guideline directing staff to study up to 0.50 cents per $100 assessed value for parks and trails maintenance and renovation. Mayor Bill Bell opposed any new parks facilities or land banking, asked staff to raise the study ceiling to 1 cent for informational options while providing tax, fee, and solid-waste subsidy comparisons across North Carolina's largest cities plus Cary and Chapel Hill, and Cole-McFadden, Brown, and Moffitt raised questions about park security, cumulative fee burdens on low-income residents, and per-capita municipal revenues. Schewel acknowledged losing his push for new facilities (6-1) and moved an amendment directing staff to prepare a parks/trails maintenance and renovation plan at funding levels up to 1 cent (incorporating Cole-McFadden's park-policing question), which passed 7-0 before the full guidelines passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (City Attorney Priority Modification): Window Installation Agreement at 112 West Main Street (Empress Development LLC)
votes.notes: Replaces original consent item language for proposed sale of air rights easement at 106 West Main Street.
votes.discussion_detail: As a priority item, the City Attorney requested modifying Consent Item 12 regarding the proposed sale of an air rights easement at 106 West Main Street to Empress Development LLC, following work session discussions. The modified motion replaced items A and B to authorize the City Manager, in return for $2,400 paid by Empress Development LLC, to execute an agreement granting the legal rights necessary to install windows in the east wall of the building at 112 West Main Street. Council moved, seconded, and approved the priority modification 7-0, effectively adopting Item 12.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-4, 8-9, 11, 13-16, excluding pulled Items 6-7 and approved Item 12)
votes.notes: Items 6 and 7 were pulled for separate discussion; Item 12 was already adopted under City Attorney priority items; voting was reopened briefly due to a malfunctioning voting button.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda titles, covering minutes (Item 1), DPAC Oversight Committee and DCVB/TDA appointments (Items 2-3), 2013 boards and commissions attendance report and February 2014 social media performance audit (Item 4), Brenda Miller Holmes public art location change (Item 8), CCB Plaza sculpture donation (Item 9), January 2014 bid report (Item 11), HUD Fair Housing Grant amendment (Item 13), USGS rainfall/streamflow agreement (Item 14), 2013 street repaving ST-265 amendment (Item 15), and NCDOT East End Connector agreements (Item 16). Councilmember Steve Schewel pulled Item 6 (budget guidelines) and Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden pulled Item 7 (rapid rehousing contract). After reopening the electronic vote because one member's button initially failed to register, Council approved the consent agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension, and Initial Zoning – Chapel Creek (BDG13-10 / Z13-14)
votes.notes: Approves utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation (BDG13-10), and initial PDR 8.00 zoning (Z13-14) for 17.1 acres near NC 54.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented the consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation (BDG13-10), and initial Planned Development Residential (PDR 8.00) zoning (Z13-14) for 17.1 acres at George King Road and Crossland Drive near NC 54, allowing up to 105 residential units with positive fiscal impact and a 12-0 Planning Commission endorsement. Eastwood Park residents Lynn Scott and Chris Selby spoke in favor of maintaining the eight-units-per-acre density cap as a buffer between single-family homes and the future Leigh Village rail station, and developer representative Jared Edens proffered $13,000 ($500 per projected student) to Durham Public Schools. Councilmember Steve Schewel thanked the applicant for the school proffer and questioned Young and Transportation staff Bill Judge on when NC 54 congestion improvements would advance through NCDOT regional prioritization. Council closed the hearing and passed the item 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7 (Pulled Consent): Third Amendment to Contract for ESG and Dedicated Housing Fund Rapid Rehousing Services with Housing for New Hope
votes.notes: Adds FY 2014 funds ($200,000 dedicated housing fund and $67,000 ESG) to Housing for New Hope contract; Council directed staff to improve outreach so competing providers like Healing with Care are notified.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden pulled Item 7 after declining to suspend rules at the work session so Healing with Care and the public could address transparency in rapid-rehousing funding allocations. Healing with Care leaders Dr. Sharon Elliott-Bynum, Darryl Hickman, Kelly Fenner, and Carolyn Hinton described housing 42 formerly homeless individuals—including veterans with health, credit, and criminal barriers—and urged equal opportunity to compete for city funds. Community Development Assistant Director Larry Jarvis clarified that Item 7 extended Housing for New Hope's existing contract with FY 2014 funds ($200,000 dedicated housing funds and $67,000 ESG) and that Housing for New Hope had been the sole applicant in the advertised FY 2015 ESG/dedicated-fund round, whereas Healing with Care had applied through the separate Continuum of Care ($108,000) process. Councilmembers Cole-McFadden, Brown, Catotti, Schewel, Davis, and Moffitt praised both organizations, urged staff to demystify funding streams and directly contact providers ahead of the fall round, and approved the amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 6 (Amendment): Amend FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines to Study Dedicated Parks and Trails Maintenance Funding up to 1 Cent
votes.notes: Modified Councilmember Schewel's initial 0.50-cent cap to 1.0 cent per $100 assessed value for maintenance and renovation of parks and trails only (no new facilities), and incorporated Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden's park policing question.
votes.discussion_detail: Councilmember Steve Schewel pulled Item 6 to add a budget guideline omitted at the work session directing staff to prepare options up to 0.50 cents per $100 assessed value for parks and trails maintenance and renovation. Mayor Bill Bell objected to any land banking or facility expansion but offered to raise the study ceiling to 1 cent for informational purposes while requesting comparative tax rates, fees, solid-waste subsidies, and parks maintenance budgets for Charlotte, Raleigh, Greensboro, Winston-Salem, Durham, Cary, and Chapel Hill. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden raised concerns over protecting park assets through policing and cumulative rate impacts on low-income residents; Eugene Brown questioned shifting the $1.85 solid waste fee into a 0.4-cent property tax; and Don Moffitt requested per-capita local revenue comparisons. Acknowledging he lacked votes (6-1) for new parks facilities, Schewel moved to amend the guidelines so staff prepare a parks and trails maintenance and renovation plan at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value (including Cole-McFadden's security question), which passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 6 (Main Motion): Adopt FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines as Amended
votes.notes: Adopts full FY 2014-2015 budget guidelines following adoption of Schewel's parks maintenance amendment.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after passing Councilmember Steve Schewel's amendment directing staff to prepare parks and trails maintenance funding scenarios up to 1 cent per $100 assessed value (along with comparative municipal tax/fee data and park security information), Council proceeded to vote on the full amended FY 2014-2015 Budget Development Guidelines. With no further discussion, the motion was properly moved and seconded and passed unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.issue: FY 2014-2015 Budget Guidelines – Scope and Tax Level of Dedicated Parks Funding ('Penny for Parks')
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether dedicated property tax funding for parks should be used for new facilities and land expansion or restricted strictly to maintenance and renovation of existing assets, and weighed tax/fee burdens on lower-income residents before settling on an informational study capped at 1 cent solely for maintenance and renovation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Limit any dedicated parks funding strictly to maintaining and renovating existing parks and trails (no new facilities or land acquisition) and study up to 1 cent alongside peer-city tax/fee and park policing data.
side_a_arguments: Existing parks and recreation facilities face severe deferred maintenance deficiencies that must be addressed before building new facilities or buying land.
Raising taxes without clear maintenance priorities, police protection of park assets, and analysis of cumulative water/sewer/stormwater/solid-waste burdens could hurt low-income residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Seek new parks facilities in addition to maintenance and renovation (initially championed by Steve Schewel before conceding a 6-1 council majority against new facilities, shifting to a 0.5-cent maintenance/renovation study).
side_b_arguments: A majority of Council still supported exploring dedicated funding for parks and trails maintenance and renovation so Council could review concrete service-level options between 0 and 0.5 cents (or up to 1 cent) during budget workshops.
Underutilized small parks could also be evaluated for repurposing rather than purely selling or abandoning.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel conceded on record that his push for new parks facilities lacked support (6-1) and moved an amended guideline—approved 7-0—directing staff to present a specific plan for parks and trails maintenance and renovation at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value.
