meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 17, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on March 17, 2014, celebrating Southern High School's 3AA state football championship, NCCU Chancellor Deborah Saunders White's upcoming installation, and NCCU's MEAC men's basketball championship alongside proclamations for Donate Life, CROP Hunger Walk, and Arbor Day. Council adopted the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 5) and then voted 6-1—with Eugene Brown dissenting—to uphold staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' $108,000 impact fee appeal after the City Attorney advised that City Code strictly required applying the 2009 fee schedule in effect when building permits were filed in 2010-2011 despite prolonged neighbor litigation. Council also held the FY 2014-2015 budget public hearing, approved the 54 Plaza annexation/CG(D) zoning and Bethpage Village committed-element revisions, adopted a memorial resolution for F.V. 'Pete' Allison Jr., authorized negotiations on $3.97 million in economic incentives for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, and approved the pulled insurance plan.

agenda_items.title: Donate Life, CROP Hunger Walk, Arbor Day, Southern High Football, and NCCU Chancellor & Basketball Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented proclamations for Donate Life Month (Sharon Hirsch), the 40th annual Durham CROP Hunger Walk (Karen Johnson), and Arbor Day marking 31 years as a Tree City USA (Assistant General Services Director Chris Boyer). Council also honored the Southern School of Energy and Sustainability football team and Coach Adrian Jones for winning the 2013 NCHSAA 3AA state championship, recognized NCCU Chancellor Dr. Deborah Saunders White's installation by ceremonially naming Fayetteville Street 'NCCU Boulevard,' and celebrated Coach LeVelle Moton and the NCCU men's basketball team for winning the 2014 MEAC tournament.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (DPAC Appointments, FY 2013-14 Budget Amendments, SAMHSA Grant, Water Facility Chemical Systems)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda excluding Item 5 (Annual Property and Casualty Insurance Plan 2014-2015), which was pulled by Victoria Peterson. Approved items included DPAC Oversight Committee appointments, FY 2013-2014 budget/grant/CIP ordinance amendments, a SAMHSA grant project ordinance and contract with Alliance Behavioral Healthcare, and a construction contract for North and South Durham Water Reclamation Facilities chemical systems.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing – Impact Fee Appeal, Phillips Research Park Apartments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson introduced an appeal under City Code Section 30-87 by Phillips Research Park Apartments seeking to apply pre-July 2009 impact fees ($108,000 lower) after neighbor Colonial's zoning appeal delayed site plan approval and caused Phillips to lose its 2008 loan before building permits were filed in 2010-2011. Attorney Robin Curren and developer Mr. Phillips argued for equitable tolling, while Planning Director Steve Medlin noted mandatory UDO stay rules and applicant-side delays, and City Attorney Patrick Baker advised Council had no legal basis in code to retroactively apply expired fees. Steve Schewel moved to uphold staff's assessment (seconded), Diane Catotti concurred, Eugene Brown urged referring back to the manager and criticized planning communication, Eddie Davis weighed splitting the fee difference, and Council voted 6-1 to uphold the staff determination with Brown voting No.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing – FY 2014-2015 Budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing to gather community input for the upcoming FY 2014-2015 budget. Seven speakers addressed Council: Victoria Peterson urged $5 million over five years for vocational-technical training at Holton School; DOST Chair LaDonna Summers urged budgeting Zone 2 impact-fee matching funds to prevent losing a nine-year-old $2 million federal rail-to-trail earmark; Vince Hammer, Donna Rudolph, John Martin, and Peter Katz of the InterNeighborhood Council advocated additional Planning Department staffing to complete the Wireless Facilities / Cell Tower Ordinance update and historic district grants; and Historic Preservation Commission Chair Heather Slane requested $2,000 for an annual historic-district newsletter.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – 54 Plaza (Utility Extension, BDG13-14, Initial Zoning Z13-21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented a consolidated utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation petition (BDG13-14), and initial Commercial General with a development plan zoning (Z13-21) for the 54 Plaza development, confirming adequate water/sewer capacity, immediate net-positive fiscal impact, and an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation. Brandon White of Kimley-Horn represented developer Durham Imperial Investors with no public opposition.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change – Bethpage Village Revisions (Z13-00030)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Steve Medlin presented committed-element revisions for Bethpage Village (PDR 4.733, IL(D), CG(D)) exempting Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) units from voluntary DPS donations, modifying recreation amenities, and addressing an existing single grave site (recommended 11-0 by the Planning Commission). In response to concerns from Councilmember Don Moffitt and Diane Catotti, applicant representative Scott Lay proffered revised committed elements guaranteeing at least one active recreation area in any non-age-restricted portion and requiring HOA maintenance and a four-foot decorative fence with gate if the grave site is not relocated under state law.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Memorializing Ferdinand Vincent 'F.V. / Pete' Allison Jr.

Mayor Bill Bell objected to contract language stating 'no specific SDBE provisions are required by ordinance' and demanded firm minority contracting goals; Steve Schewel questioned how many of the 500 office jobs were relocated from Duke versus new, the gap between $71.5M taxable investment and $60.9M assessed value, Year 1 net fiscal return, combined city-county leverage ratio, livable wage, and minority hiring; and Cora Cole-McFadden pressed for summer youth employment participation (which Dick confirmed was embedded in the workforce plan).

disagreements.issue: Phillips Research Park Apartments Impact Fee Appeal – Strict Code Enforcement vs. Equitable Tolling for Neighbor Litigation Delays
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 in upholding staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' appeal of a $108,000 impact fee increase incurred after a competitor's zoning appeals froze the project from 2008 until building permits were filed under the higher 2009 fee schedule, with Eugene Brown dissenting and Eddie Davis exploring a compromise split.
disagreements.side_a_position: Uphold the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule in effect when the building permit application was submitted.
side_a_arguments: City Code strictly mandates that impact fees be calculated at the time a completed building permit application is submitted (here 2010-2011), leaving Council and the Impact Fee Appeal Committee no legal authority to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates.
While the neighboring competitor's appeals caused hardship, Planning staff followed mandatory UDO stay provisions and the application also sat with the developer for extended periods.
Granting retroactive fee relief to one developer could expose the city to legal challenges and refund demands from other developers affected by fee or regulatory changes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the appeal back to the City Manager rather than upholding the higher 2009 fee assessment, citing inadequate Planning Department communication and notification to the developer.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff failed to communicate effectively with the developer regarding the impact fee change and could have communicated more forcefully regarding the neighboring owner's interconnection obligations.

Because the developer relied on 2007 staff reliance letters, closed a $23 million loan in 2008, and was stalled by third-party litigation outside its control, Council should send the matter back to the Manager for further review rather than deny relief.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel's motion to uphold the staff and Impact Fee Appeal Committee determination passed 6-1, with Councilmember Eugene Brown voting No (while Councilmember Eddie Davis noted he would have favored splitting the increase in half if legally permissible but did not offer a substitute motion after Schewel's motion carried).

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Rescheduled to Thursday afternoon at 4:30 p.m. after Monday's regular meeting was canceled and conducted briskly due to sleet outside, the Durham City Council approved the City Manager's priority deferrals of the FY 2014-2015 budget/CIP hearing and two land-use hearings to March 17, 2014. The Council unanimously adopted the 13-item Consent Agenda (including boards and commissions appointments, a performance audit, and infrastructure and sidewalk contracts) and approved General Business Item 19 without discussion. Police Chief Jose Lopez then delivered the Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report, highlighting national CALEA and forensic accreditations, a 6% drop in Part 1 violent crime (including a 23-year low in robberies), and a 6% increase in property crime driven by larcenies.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Weather Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the rescheduled March 6, 2014 meeting to order at 4:30 p.m., noting that Monday's meeting had been canceled and that council had already held work and closed sessions earlier in the day. All seven council members answered roll call. Mayor Bell announced that sleet was falling outside and urged council to move expeditiously for the safety of staff and attendees, adding that Southern High School's football team would be recognized on March 17.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items: Crime Report Presentation and Deferrals to March 17, 2014
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager's office requested to present supplemental Item 22 (Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report) during the meeting and to defer three public hearing items to March 17, 2014: Item 15 (FY 2014-2015 budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan), Item 16 (54 Plaza consolidated annexation), and Item 17 (Bethpage Village Revisions zoning map change Z1300030). Neither the City Attorney nor the City Clerk had priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Appointments, Performance Audit, Infrastructure & Stormwater Contracts, Q2 Financial Report)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the titles of Consent Agenda Items 1 through 13, covering minutes approval, appointments to the Appearance, Open Space and Trails, and Planning Commissions, street and infrastructure acceptances, a performance audit of inventory controls for tools and safety materials, Carver Street Extension right-of-way acquisition, DPR operations facility architectural amendment, Third Fork Creek stream restoration, ditching/pipe replacement, Garrett Road sidewalk construction, NCDOT Schedule C and D agreements, and the FY 2013-2014 Q2 financial report. No items were pulled by council or the public.

agenda_items.title: General Business Agenda Item 19
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following confirmation that public hearings Items 15 through 17 were deferred to March 17, 2014, Council took up General Business Agenda Item 19 without separate staff presentation or public comment. A motion to approve was immediately made, seconded, and carried unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez presented the 2013 annual crime summary, highlighting DPD's CALEA Gold Standard Accreditation, Forensics Services Division ISO accreditation, and outreach initiatives including the RAP burglary prevention program and mental health CIT outreach. Chief Lopez reported that Part 1 violent crime fell 6% in 2013 with robberies at a 23-year low and 30 criminal homicides (12 open), while property crime rose 6% due to larcenies (mostly thefts from vehicles and shoplifting), sworn staffing stood at 99% full at year-end, and average Priority 1 response time was 5.9 minutes against a 5.8-minute target. Council Member Don Moffitt noted the executive summary was missing from the packet and asked Chief Lopez to clarify the expanded FBI definition of rape (which accounted for the 40% statistical increase while prior-definition numbers held steady at 73) and the distinction between burglary and robbery.

agenda_items.title: Poverty Reduction Initiative Announcement and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell reminded council and the public about a follow-up meeting on his neighborhood-by-neighborhood poverty reduction initiative scheduled for March 19 from 7:30 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. at the Durham Rescue Mission, noting invitation letters had been sent to neighborhood associations. With no further business, the meeting adjourned at 4:49 p.m.

votes.item_title: City Manager's Priority Items (Present Item 22 Crime Report; Defer Items 15, 16, and 17 to March 17, 2014)
votes.notes: Deferred Item 15 (FY14-15 budget & FY15-20 CIP public hearing), Item 16 (54 Plaza annexation), and Item 17 (Bethpage Village Revisions Z1300030) to March 17, 2014; added Item 22 DPD Crime Report presentation.
votes.discussion_detail: Due to the rescheduling of the regular Monday council meeting to Thursday, March 6 at 4:30 p.m. and inclement sleet conditions, the City Manager's office proposed deferring three major public hearing items—the FY 2014-2015 budget and FY 2015-2020 CIP hearing (Item 15), the 54 Plaza consolidated annexation (Item 16), and the Bethpage Village Revisions rezoning Z1300030 (Item 17)—to the March 17, 2014 regular meeting. Staff requested to proceed only with presenting Supplemental Item 22, the Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report. No council members raised objections or requested discussion. Council unanimously approved the priority items 7-0.

votes.item_title: General Business Agenda Item 19
votes.notes: General Business Agenda Item 19 (not deferred; specific title not read aloud in transcript).
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following adoption of the Consent Agenda, Mayor Bill Bell called General Business Agenda Item 19 for action. No staff presentation, council questions, or public remarks were offered on the item, consistent with Mayor Bell's opening request to move swiftly because of worsening sleet outside. A motion to approve Item 19 was properly moved and seconded. The Council voted 7-0 to approve the item.

meetings.title: Durham City Council February 17, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting with six members present and one excused, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Items 3 and 5) and deferred Item 3 (the roadside solicitation ordinance) to Thursday's work session following public comments and sharp council debate over panhandling enforcement versus social support. Council then approved Item 5—a ground lease agreement and parking fee ordinance for a Ninth Street lot taking effect June 1, 2014 after a three-month rent-free improvement window—and unanimously passed two public hearing land-use items: revising the 1997 Durham-Morrisville annexation agreement for the 7-acre O'Brien property and approving the consolidated annexation and initial RR zoning for Farrington Road Baptist Church.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Excused Absence, and Snowstorm Staff Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the meeting to order, Council Member Eddie Davis led the Pledge of Allegiance, and Council voted 6-0 during roll call to excuse one absent member. Council postponed recognizing Southern High School's state championship football team because team members were not present. Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden announced Friday's Human Relations Awards at the Hayti Heritage Center and requested a review of the city's inclement-weather employee attendance policy, while Council Member Don Moffitt praised Public Works, Police, Fire, Solid Waste, General Services, and Fleet Management staff for 24/7 work during the recent snowstorm.

agenda_items.title: Roadside Solicitation Ordinance (Referred to Thursday Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney noted technical edits remained on one-way street solicitation from the driver's side, and Mayor Bell asked to refer the ordinance to Thursday's work session so he could share Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residential areas near parks and streets from intimidation. Speakers offered contrasting views: Carolyn Schul of Principle Ministry lamented a year of postponements harming people who rely on begging for sustenance, while Victoria Peterson urged action against clusters of panhandlers hurting African-American businesses along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue. Council Member Steve Schewel urged moving forward after a year of consensus work, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden argued the city needed to transform lives rather than merely allow begging, and Council voted 6-0 to defer to Thursday.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 3 and 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After briefly reading from an outdated agenda before correcting to the current docket, Mayor Bell read the Consent Agenda covering minutes, December 2013 bid report, ESRI software maintenance, MLK Jr. Parkway and Archdale Drive traffic signal and cable installation, NCDOT Section 5303 MPO grant, Civic Software DCHC MPO website redevelopment, and North Durham Water Reclamation Facility roof replacement. Item 3 (Roadside Solicitation) and Item 5 (Ninth Street Ground Lease) were pulled for discussion, and the remainder passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Ground Lease Agreement (CP GPI Regency) and Ninth Street Parking Lot Fee Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Mark Ahrendsen presented a revised agreement for the Ninth Street parking lot in which the lease begins March 1, 2014 but both lease payments and $1 parking fees are delayed until June 1, 2014 while the developer performs up to $30,000 in milling and striping. Ahrendsen confirmed multi-space pay stations would accept coins, currency, credit cards, and cell-phone extensions, and noted staff was working with Duke on Alley 8 improvements and OEWD on a Ninth Street business grant program. Council Member Don Moffitt requested a 45- or 90-day status report on merchant and employee parking outreach across Ninth, Perry, and Irondale Streets, and Council Member Steve Schewel thanked staff and the developer before unanimous approval.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Morrisville Annexation Agreement Revision (O'Brien Property)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Pat Young presented a requested amendment to the 1997 Durham-Morrisville annexation agreement transferring approximately seven acres (the O'Brien property, part of KCR Developers' Kitts Creek development in Wake County/Morrisville) from Durham's annexation area to Morrisville's, effective April 1, 2014, because serving it from Durham would require a costly stream-buffer crossing on Distribution Drive. Attorney Patrick Byker spoke in support on behalf of KCR Developers LLC. Council Member Steve Schewel asked how areas of Morrisville, Chapel Hill, and Raleigh inside Durham County would be affected by any future City-County merger, with staff noting those municipalities would have to be part of merger negotiations.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation: Farrington Road Baptist Church (6004 Farrington Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a voluntary annexation, utility extension, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning request for roughly eight acres at 6004 Farrington Road to allow Farrington Road Baptist Church to pursue a minor special use permit for an approximately 24,000-square-foot place of worship. Applicant representative Stark noted the church was relocating south across NC 54 near Falconbridge and that engineer Phil Cook was available. Council Member Steve Schewel questioned how Budget and Management Services' fiscal impact model projected significant sales tax revenue for a tax-exempt relocated church, and staff agreed to follow up with Budget Director Bertha Johnson.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Absent Council Member
votes.notes: 6-0 vote during roll call to excuse 1 absent council member; Mayor Bill Bell, Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden, Council Member Don Moffitt, and Council Member Steve Schewel are confirmed present in the transcript, with 2 of the remaining 3 seated members also present.
votes.discussion_detail: During the opening roll call conducted by the City Clerk, Council paused to consider an excused absence request for one absent member of the seven-member Council. A motion to grant the excused absence was properly moved and seconded without discussion. The Clerk opened and closed the vote, recording a unanimous 6-0 tally among the members present. The six present members proceeded to conduct all business for the remainder of the evening.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Approval (Excluding Pulled Items 3 and 5)
votes.notes: Approved Items 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9 (minutes, Dec 2013 bid report, ESRI software maintenance, MLK Jr. Pkwy/Archdale Dr traffic signal, NCDOT Section 5303 grant, Civic Software DCHC MPO website, North Durham WRF roof replacement); Items 3 and 5 were pulled for separate consideration.
votes.discussion_detail: After locating the current meeting agenda, Mayor Bill Bell read aloud the Consent Agenda items covering administrative minutes, purchasing reports, technology maintenance, transportation grants and signalization, and water reclamation facility maintenance. Item 3 (Roadside Solicitation) and Item 5 (Ninth Street ground lease and parking fees) were pulled for separate discussion due to council questions and public speakers present. Council then moved and seconded adoption of the remaining Consent Agenda items. The motion carried unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 3: Refer Roadside Solicitation Ordinance to Thursday Work Session
votes.notes: Referred Item 3 back to Thursday's work session so the City Attorney can finalize one-way street driver-side solicitation language and Mayor Bell can present Springfield, Missouri residential protection measures.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney reported that staff was still drafting a work-session revision allowing solicitation from the driver's side on one-way streets and offered council the choice of referring Item 3 to Thursday's work session or passing it with a pending amendment, noting any ordinance would not take effect for 30 days. Mayor Bell requested referral to Thursday so council could examine Springfield, Missouri's approach to protecting residents living near parks and intersections from intimidation. Two speakers addressed the council: Carolyn Schul of Principle Ministry criticized a year of repeated delays hurting people who depend on panhandling for survival, while resident Victoria Peterson urged the city to address large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue that deter customers from Black-owned businesses. Council Member Steve Schewel urged timely passage after extensive collaboration with police, attorneys, and HSAC, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden contended the city should focus on transforming lives and ending panhandling rather than enabling it. Council voted 6-0 to refer the item to Thursday's work session.

votes.item_title: Item 5: Ground Lease Agreement (CP GPI Regency) and Ninth Street Parking Lot Fee Ordinance
votes.notes: Lease begins March 1, 2014 with three-month payment deferral until June 1, 2014; includes $1 parking rate via numbered-space pay stations.
votes.discussion_detail: Transportation Director Mark Ahrendsen explained that following council concerns at the prior work session, the property owner agreed to delay lease payments and the $1 parking fee ordinance from March 1 to June 1, 2014 while the developer completes up to $30,000 in lot milling and striping. Ahrendsen clarified that numbered parking spaces would use multi-payment pay stations accepting coins, cash, credit cards, and cell-phone extensions, and reported ongoing coordination with Duke University on Alley 8 and OEWD on a Ninth Street business grant program slated for April. Council Member Don Moffitt sought assurance that staff outreach would include merchants on Perry and Irondale Streets and requested a 45- or 90-day progress report on employee parking options raised by merchant Tom Campbell. Council Member Steve Schewel commended staff and the developer for addressing merchant concerns, and Council approved the agreement and amended effective date 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Durham-Morrisville Annexation Agreement Revision (O'Brien Property)
votes.notes: Transfers ~7 acres (O'Brien property) from Durham's annexation area to Morrisville's annexation area effective April 1, 2014.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented a requested amendment to the 1997 interlocal annexation agreement with the Town of Morrisville to move roughly seven acres—the O'Brien property, part of the larger Kitts Creek project in Morrisville and Wake County—into Morrisville's annexation area effective April 1, 2014. Young explained that Water Management, Public Works, and Finance found no detrimental impact and noted Durham service would require a costly, environmentally sensitive stream-buffer crossing to extend Distribution Drive. Attorney Patrick Byker spoke briefly on behalf of KCR Developers LLC in support of the staff recommendation. Responding to a question from Council Member Steve Schewel about how Morrisville, Chapel Hill, and Raleigh parcels inside Durham County would be treated in any future city-county merger, Young stated those towns would need to participate in merger negotiations; the public hearing closed and Council approved the revision 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 14: Consolidated Annexation and Initial RR Zoning — Farrington Road Baptist Church
votes.notes: Voluntary annexation, utility extension, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for ~8 acres at 6004 Farrington Road for a proposed ~24,000 sq ft church.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Farrington Road Baptist Church's petition for voluntary annexation, utility extension, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning on approximately eight acres at 6004 Farrington Road to facilitate a roughly 24,000-square-foot sanctuary subject to a future Board of Adjustment minor special use permit. Staff confirmed adequate utilities and reported a positive fiscal impact analysis, while applicant representative Stark noted the congregation was simply relocating across NC 54 near Falconbridge. Council Member Steve Schewel questioned the attachment's cost-benefit model, noting property taxes were properly excluded for a tax-exempt church while expressing skepticism over seemingly high projected sales tax revenues for a relocated church. Young acknowledged the model used pro-rata non-residential estimates and promised to have Budget Management Services review the calibration, after which Council closed the hearing and approved the annexation and zoning 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Delaying vs. Enacting Revisions to the Roadside Solicitation (Panhandling) Ordinance (Item 3)
disagreements.summary: Public speakers and council members differed over whether to refer the revised roadside solicitation ordinance back to work session for additional residential-protection rules or enact it after a year of deliberation, as well as over the city's broader approach to panhandling.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move forward promptly with the consensus ordinance revision and allow regulated solicitation so impoverished residents are not further harmed by delays.
side_a_arguments: Stakeholders, police, the city attorney's office, and the Homeless Services Advisory Committee subcommittee spent over a year developing an alternative and reaching consensus.
Repeated postponements prolong hardship for individuals who rely on begging for sustenance (Carolyn Schul).
disagreements.side_b_position: Refer the ordinance back to work session to add residential protections and address ongoing neighborhood and business impacts rather than continuing to permit street begging.
side_b_arguments: Technical adjustments for driver-side solicitation on one-way streets were still unfinished, and Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residents living near parks and intersections needed review (Bill Bell).
Large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue hurt African-American business districts (Victoria Peterson).
Permitting solicitation fails to transform lives or end panhandling, and the city should pursue different strategies to connect people with resources (Cora Cole-McFadden).
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 6-0 to refer Item 3 to the Thursday work session for further review.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell opened the evening with his 12th Annual State of the City Address, launching a 2014 citywide priority to reduce Durham's roughly 21% poverty rate neighborhood by neighborhood through coordinated partnerships such as End Poverty Durham/REAL Durham, Made in Durham, and the East Durham Children's Initiative. In regular business, Council recognized Human Relations Month and memorialized late civil rights leader Joseph W. A. Becton, Jr., approved the Consent Agenda (referring Item 5 back to staff), and unanimously passed the Clover Hill Place street-paving assessment roll as well as three land-use cases (Ellis Road Residential plan amendment and rezoning for 90 townhomes, and Croasdaile Commons rezoning). Council then held extensive debates on two developer-initiated UDO text amendments by Horvath Associates, adopting Article 6 density revisions 7-0 while continuing the tree-coverage easement calculation amendment (TC1300002) to May 19, 2014 for parcel modeling after environmental advocates and Council Member Steve Schewel objected to its impact on large tracts.

agenda_items.title: Mayor Bill Bell's 12th Annual State of the City Address
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a 2013 year-in-review video, Mayor Bill Bell delivered his 12th State of the City Address, noting violent crime fell 5.6% while property crime rose nearly 6%, and proposing a signature 2014 initiative to reduce poverty in Durham neighborhood by neighborhood. Citing UNC Poverty Center data showing 21% citywide poverty and 37.5% to 50% poverty in East Durham census tracts, he highlighted community partners including End Poverty Durham and REAL Durham (Rev. Mel Williams and Cameron Smith), Made in Durham (Dr. Victor Dzau, Chancellor Deborah Saunders-White, and City Manager Tom Bonfield), East Durham Children's Initiative (David Reese, Barker French, and resident Ms. Bass), and Durham County Public Health (Gail Harris).

agenda_items.title: Human Relations Month Proclamation and Resolution Memorializing Joseph W. A. Becton, Jr.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Don Moffitt presented a proclamation declaring February 2014 Human Relations Month to Human Relations Commission Chair Ricky Hart, Vice Chair Phil Seib, and Director Delilah Donaldson, inviting residents to the February 21 Human Relations Awards ceremony featuring keynote speaker Mandy Carter. Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden then presented a formal memorial resolution honoring former Human Relations Executive Director and civil rights leader Joseph William Anderson Becton, Jr. (1932–2013) to his widow Edna Ray Becton and family, reflecting on his role in Durham's fair housing ordinance and his historic alliance with Ann Atwater and C.P. Ellis.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Item (Refer Item 5) and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested referring Item 5 (Main Street Bridge Replacement waterline utility agreement with NCDOT) back to the administration, which Council approved 7-0. Council then unanimously approved the remaining Consent Agenda items covering street/infrastructure acceptances, a SAMHSA grant ordinance amendment, deputy finance officer appointment/removal, annual and sick leave code modifications, Duke Energy pole replacement for the Alston/East Durham streetscape, light transit vehicle conversion, and the DCHC MPO memorandum of understanding.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Roll for Street Paving — Clover Hill Place (Dunwoody Subdivision)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff member Robert Joyner presented the confirmation of the assessment roll for completed street paving improvements on Clover Hill Place in the Dunwoody Subdivision. With no council questions or public speakers during the public hearing, Council closed the hearing and confirmed the assessment roll.

agenda_items.title: Ellis Road Residential Comprehensive Plan Amendment (A1300008) and Zoning Map Change (Z1300026)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Pat Young presented companion requests from T. Hankins Development to redesignate 15.53 acres at 1443 Ellis Road from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential and rezone it from RS-20 to PDR 7.341 for 90 townhomes, including a bicycle-lane dedication and cross-access. Applicant representative Jared Edens proffered $500 to Durham Public Schools prior to first final plat to offset one projected student, and Council Member Steve Schewel confirmed UDO steep-slope protections would be field-verified at site plan; both items passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Croasdaile Commons (Z1300024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a request to rezone 8.8 acres at Croasdaile Commons on Hillandale Road from Commercial Center (CC) to Commercial General with a development plan (CG(D)) to allow approximately 11,000 additional square feet of office use. Council Member Steve Schewel inquired why no bike lane was required along Front Street (staff explained there were no associated roadway access improvements to create a nexus) and praised the redevelopment of the shopping center; George Stancil appeared for questions and Council approved 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment — Density Revisions to Article 6 (TC1200012)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Michael Stock presented a privately initiated text amendment by Horvath Associates adjusting fractional density limits (up by at most 0.5 units/acre in OI/GC districts), extending the 1-unit/acre major roadway bonus to service roads with direct access and non-residential districts in suburban/compact tiers, and permitting higher RSM/RUM densities only via council-approved development plans. Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil supported the change to spur urban infill and corridor redevelopment, while Pat Carstensen of the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed the residential density provisions unless tied to transit and walkability. Council Member Don Moffitt questioned whether raising baseline densities weakened affordable housing density bonuses (Steve Medlin agreed current density bonuses alone were unworkable and pledged broader incentives), and Council Member Eddie Davis asked about delaying residential changes before Council unanimously approved 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment — Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michael Stock presented a second Horvath Associates text amendment exempting existing utility easements 50 feet or wider from gross development acreage when calculating suburban residential tree-coverage requirements. Proponents Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil argued wide transmission easements like the 350-foot corridor at Del Webb's Carolina Arbors prohibit tree planting and inflate housing costs, while opponents Will Wilson, Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen, and John Tarantino warned the change degrades urban public health and watersheds while letting developers retain full density and impervious surface credits from the easement. Council Member Steve Schewel said he could not support a universal exemption for large tracts, Don Moffitt suggested parcel-size or percentage thresholds, and Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014 for parcel modeling.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Item: Refer Item 5 (Main Street Bridge Replacement Waterline Agreement) Back to Administration
votes.notes: Referred Agenda Item 5 back to city administration.
votes.discussion_detail: Following ceremonial presentations, City Manager Tom Bonfield presented one priority item requesting that Agenda Item 5—the Main Street Bridge Replacement waterline utility agreement with the North Carolina Department of Transportation—be referred back to the administration. No council members questioned the referral or asked to keep the item on the agenda. A motion to approve the City Manager's priority referral was properly moved and seconded. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to refer Item 5 back to staff.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Confirmation of Assessment Roll for Street Paving — Clover Hill Place (Dunwoody Subdivision)
votes.notes: Confirms street paving assessment roll for completed improvements on Clover Hill Place.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works representative Robert Joyner presented Item 11, requesting confirmation of the assessment roll for completed street paving improvements on Clover Hill Place in the Dunwoody subdivision. Staff recommended confirming the assessment roll as presented. Mayor Bell opened the public hearing and called for council questions and public comment, but no one signed up or stepped forward to speak. After closing the public hearing, Council moved, seconded, and unanimously confirmed the assessment roll by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Ellis Road Residential (A1300008)
votes.notes: Amends Future Land Use Map for ~15.5 acres at Ellis Road from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young of the Planning Department presented Case A1300008 on behalf of T. Hankins Development to amend the Future Land Use Map for roughly 15.5 acres on the east side of Ellis Road from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential, noting it met all four UDO criteria and received a 12-0 Planning Commission recommendation. Applicant representative Jared Edens testified that the site near RTP would transition between apartments to the south and single-family homes to the north while introducing townhomes, had drawn no opposition at its September 3 neighborhood meeting, and proffered $500 to Durham Public Schools to offset one projected student. No opponents spoke during the public hearing. Following closure of the hearing, Council unanimously approved the plan amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Zoning Map Change — Ellis Road Residential (Z1300026)
votes.notes: Rezones 15.53 acres at 1443 Ellis Road from RS-20 to PDR 7.341 for 90 committed townhouse units.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented the companion rezoning (Z1300026) for 15.53 acres at 1443 Ellis Road from RS-20 to Planned Development Residential (PDR 7.341) for 90 committed townhomes, highlighting commitments for single Ellis Road access, northern cross-access, one stream crossing, bicycle-lane roadway improvements, and the $500 school proffer offered during the prior item. No public speakers opposed the request, and Jared Edens waived further remarks. Council Member Steve Schewel asked staff how steep slopes shown on the development plan would be regulated, and Young confirmed UDO steep-slope restrictions would be field-verified and enforced at site plan to bar development on qualifying slopes. Council then approved the rezoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 14: Zoning Map Change — Croasdaile Commons (Z1300024)
votes.notes: Rezones 8.8 acres at Croasdaile Commons on Hillandale Road from CC to CG(D) to permit ~11,000 additional sq ft of office use.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case Z1300024 to rezone 8.8 acres at Croasdaile Commons on Hillandale Road from Commercial Center (CC) to Commercial General with a development plan (CG(D)) to allow approximately 11,000 additional square feet of office space, noting unanimous 12-0 Planning Commission support. Council Member Steve Schewel asked why a Front Street bike lane was not included, and Young explained Transportation only seeks bike lanes when a project triggers roadway access improvements establishing a legal nexus. Schewel also praised the shopping center's redevelopment and new tenants as a strong neighborhood asset. Applicant representative George Stancil stood for questions, no opponents spoke, and Council passed the rezoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: UDO Text Amendment — Density Revisions to Article 6 (TC1200012)
votes.notes: Privately initiated UDO text amendment by Horvath Associates rounding fractional densities and extending corridor density bonuses.
votes.discussion_detail: Michael Stock presented TC1200012, a revised Horvath Associates text amendment rounding fractional densities (e.g., from 10.5 to 11 units/acre in GC/OI), extending major roadway bonuses to service roads with access and non-residential districts in suburban compact tiers, and allowing higher RSM/RUM densities only with council-approved development plans. Proponents Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil argued the modest increases encourage mixed-use infill along thoroughfares like US 15-501 and Roxboro Road, while Pat Carstensen of the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed the residential provisions as untethered to transit and walkability. Council Member Don Moffitt questioned whether raising base densities would further undercut affordable housing density bonuses, prompting Planning Director Steve Medlin to acknowledge current UDO density bonuses alone were unworkable and commit to pursuing broader cost-reducing incentives. After staff clarified to Council Member Eddie Davis that delaying the residential piece lacked clear policy direction and after Moffitt thanked Horvath and citizen reviewers for refining the text, Moffitt moved approval and Council voted 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 16: UDO Text Amendment — Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002) — Continue Public Hearing to May 19, 2014
votes.notes: Reopened and continued the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and applicant Horvath Associates can model acreage thresholds and affected parcels.
votes.discussion_detail: Michael Stock presented TC1300002, a Horvath Associates proposal excluding utility easements 50 feet or wider from gross tract area when calculating suburban residential tree coverage, which Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil argued unfairly penalized projects like the 400-acre Del Webb Carolina Arbors site crossed by a 350-foot power easement. Environmental advocates Will Wilson, Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen, and John Tarantino (paraphrasing Joni Mitchell) strongly opposed the amendment, warning it reduces urban canopy and respiratory health benefits, lets developers count easements for density and imperviousness while shedding tree requirements, and lacks parcel mapping along New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River. Council Member Steve Schewel stated he could not support a universal exemption for large tracts, while Council Member Don Moffitt floated limiting relief by tract acreage or easement percentage and Council Member Diane Catotti asked staff whether targeted thresholds were feasible within 90 days. After Mayor Bell emphasized that requesting additional modeling did not commit council to eventual approval, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014.

disagreements.issue: Article 6 UDO Density Revisions and Impact on Transit-Oriented Growth & Affordable Housing (TC1200012)
disagreements.summary: During the public hearing on Item 15, the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed residential density increases unrelated to transit access, and Council Members Don Moffitt and Eddie Davis scrutinized whether raising baseline densities undermined affordable housing bonuses or warranted delaying residential provisions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the revised Article 6 density adjustments and corridor bonuses as proposed by Horvath Associates and Planning staff.
side_a_arguments: Rounding fractional densities (at most 0.5 units/acre) and extending roadway bonuses to service roads and commercial/office districts encourages mixed-use redevelopment along major corridors.
Any higher density in RSM/RUM districts still requires a development plan approved by City Council, and service-road bonuses require direct access.
Density bonuses in the UDO can stack cumulatively, and affordable housing requires broader tools beyond density alone (Steve Medlin).
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay or reject the residential density provisions until density is directed toward walkable, transit-served areas and affordable housing bonuses are protected.
side_b_arguments: Allowing extra residential density outside transit corridors risks car-dependent sprawl (Pat Carstensen / Inter-Neighborhood Council).
Increasing by-right or baseline unit counts could reduce developers' incentive to use the affordable housing density bonus (questioned by Don Moffitt).
disagreements.resolution: Following staff clarifications that development plans still come before Council and that Planning will pursue non-density affordable housing incentives, Council unanimously approved TC1200012 by a 7-0 vote.

disagreements.issue: Excluding Wide Utility Easements from Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002)
disagreements.summary: Council and public speakers divided sharply over Horvath Associates' proposal to exclude utility easements of 50 feet or wider from tree-coverage calculations while still counting those easements toward residential density and impervious-surface allowances.
disagreements.side_a_position: Exclude wide utility easements (minus the first 50 feet) from gross tract area when calculating required tree coverage.
side_a_arguments: Power companies prohibit tree planting in wide transmission easements, forcing developers to set aside extra buildable acreage (e.g., 7.5 acres at Del Webb Carolina Arbors) to meet tree-coverage minimums.
Existing UDO exemptions already exclude ponds and road-widening rights-of-way where trees cannot be planted.
Preserving usable acreage lowers site development costs and improves housing affordability (Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, George Stancil).
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject or restrict the universal easement exemption so tree canopy is not reduced on large developments or near sensitive watersheds without parcel-level analysis.
side_b_arguments: Developers continue to receive full density and impervious-surface credit from the easement while shedding the corresponding tree-coverage obligation, harming air quality and raising urban temperatures (Will Wilson, Steve Schewel).
Staff had not mapped affected parcels near protected watersheds such as New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River (Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen).
While small tracts encumbered by wide power easements might merit relief, there is no clear public interest in reducing tree requirements for very large developments (Steve Schewel).
disagreements.resolution: Unable to support the text amendment as drafted, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and the applicant could map affected parcels and model tract-size or percentage thresholds.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting January 21, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presiding in Mayor Bill Bell's excused absence and snow/sleet outside, the Durham City Council expedited a 6-0 unanimous slate of major economic, land-use, and parking actions. Council approved a $600,000 capital-investment incentive contract with biopharmaceutical firm Argos Therapeutics (projected to add 178 jobs and $1.69 million in net tax revenue over 10 years), passed the Montclair Phase II annexation and 24-home rezoning over a neighbor's request for a 1,000-foot chain-link fence, and approved the Meadows at Southpoint II plan amendment and 185-unit rezoning with a vinyl-siding ban and $500 school proffer. On pulled Consent Item 5, following downtown residents' protests over ending free parking and legal advice against retroactive 2008 cutoffs, Council compromised 6-0 on a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Mayor's Excused Absence, and Civil Rights Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m., announced the Joseph Becton memorial resolution was held due to snow and sleet, and Council voted 6-0 to grant Mayor Bill Bell an excused absence to attend the U.S. Conference of Mayors meeting. Council Member Don Moffitt commended DPD's restraint during Sunday protests and noted the MLK march, while Council Member Eddie Davis recognized Royal Ice Cream sit-in participant Virginia Williams and documentarian Dr. Steve Channing following a New York Times obituary of Franklin McCain.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cole-McFadden read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 4 covering City Council minutes, 2013 municipal primary and election items with the Durham County Board of Elections, and two Workforce Investment Act contracts with Educational Data Systems, Inc. Item 5 (Ordinance to Change Parking Fees) was pulled to be heard after the public hearings, and Items 1 through 4 passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Contract — Argos Therapeutics, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD's Kevin Dick presented a $600,000, seven-year performance-based capital investment incentive for biopharmaceutical firm Argos Therapeutics on Alexander Drive, noting projected net tax revenue of $1.69 million over 10 years, an increased commitment from 118 to 178 net new jobs over three years, and workforce/local-business recruitment plans. Chamber of Commerce representative Ted Connor and NCCU BRITE Center's Dr. Li-An Yeh joined Argos officials in support, highlighting personalized kidney cancer immunotherapies and local hiring. Council praised Durham County's matching role and the project's job quality, passing the contract 6-0 by voice vote after the electronic system failed to register.

agenda_items.title: Montclair Phase II — Utility Extension, Voluntary Annexation, and Initial Zoning (14.89 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented three companion actions for Montclair Phase II (Barbee Chapel and Farrington Mill Roads) to annex and zone 14.89 acres PDR 2.00/RR for up to 24 single-family homes, correcting the annexation ordinance effective date to March 31, 2014. Applicant Jared Edens (for David Weekley Homes) proffered $1,500 to Durham Public Schools prior to final plat and a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the property line with neighbor Michael Hining, who opposed the project without a 1,000-foot chain-link fence to keep children away from his farm ponds and fruit trees. After Council Member Steve Schewel noted the difficulty of deciding on the fence, Council passed all three actions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Meadows at Southpoint II (A1300007)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case A1300007 by Meadows Land Investment LLC to amend the Future Land Use Map for 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from Office and Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential, which Planning Commission recommended 13-1. Hunter's Wood neighborhood representative George Bryan and applicant attorney Ken Spaulding spoke in support of the residential designation, and Council approved the amendment 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Meadows at Southpoint II (Z1300020)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case Z1300020 rezoning 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from RR and OI to PDR 4.718 for up to 185 residential units with stormwater aeration, a 100-foot perimeter buffer, bike-lane asphalt, a bus pull-out/shelter, and road improvements. George Bryan supported the owner-occupied townhome shift but requested changing the full-access Barbee Road driveway to right-in/right-out or adding warning signs; Transportation's Bill Judge explained sight-distance constraints were to the left so right-in/right-out would not resolve them and NCDOT would enforce sight-distance and signage at site plan. At Council Member Diane Catotti's prompting (reflecting Mayor Bell's prior request), applicant Jim Anderson and George Stancil agreed to prohibit vinyl siding in favor of cementitious siding, and Council Member Steve Schewel secured a $500 school proffer prior to approval.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance to Change Downtown Parking Fees (5-Year Half-Price Phase-In for Current Residents)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled from the Consent Agenda by downtown residents William 'Coke' Ariail and Kate Dobbs, who argued ending free parking broke a city promise and imposed financial hardship on early downtown homeowners. City Attorney Patrick Baker advised that distinguishing pre-2008 'pioneer' residents from post-2008 residents would be legally arbitrary and capricious, whereas treating all current residents alike as a phase-out group distinct from future residents was defensible under local legislation. Transportation's Mark Ahrendsen also noted the Corcoran Street deck and surface lot operated as one facility, though Council Member Don Moffitt urged surface-lot pricing and a 10-year phase-in; Council compromised on Moffitt's motion (seconded by Steve Schewel) extending Option 2's 50% discount from three years to five years through December 31, 2018.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Mayor Bill Bell
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell absent on excused absence attending the U.S. Conference of Mayors annual meeting; Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presided.
votes.discussion_detail: During roll call at the start of the meeting, the City Clerk reported that Mayor Bill Bell had requested an excused absence to attend the U.S. Conference of Mayors annual meeting. With Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presiding in the chair, a motion to grant Mayor Bell an excused absence was moved and seconded without objection. The Clerk opened and closed the vote, recording a unanimous 6-0 tally of all seated council members present. Mayor Bell remained absent for the duration of the meeting.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-4, Excluding Pulled Item 5)
votes.notes: Approved Items 1-4 (minutes, 2013 municipal election/Board of Elections, and two WIA contracts with Educational Data Systems Inc.); Item 5 (downtown parking fees) was pulled for discussion after public hearings.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 5, noting that Item 5 (the ordinance to change downtown parking fees) had been pulled by members of the public to be heard at the end of the General Business public hearings. The remaining four items covered approval of council minutes, municipal election administration with the Durham County Board of Elections, and two Workforce Investment Act contracts with Educational Data Systems, Inc. No council members requested to pull any additional items. A motion to adopt Items 1 through 4 was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 6: Economic Development Incentive Agreement — Argos Therapeutics, Inc.
votes.notes: $600,000 performance-based capital investment payout over 7 years from incremental tax revenue; electronic voting console malfunctioned so Council took a voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Kevin Dick of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented the revised incentive agreement with Argos Therapeutics for an expansion off Alexander Drive, reporting that the company increased its three-year job creation target from 118 to 178 net new jobs while projected 10-year net city tax revenue stood at $1.69 million. The $600,000 payout over seven years would come strictly from incremental tax revenue only after building completion and job creation milestones are verified, alongside a workforce recruitment plan with the Durham Career Center and local contractor outreach. Ted Connor of the Durham Chamber of Commerce and Dr. Li-An Yeh of NCCU's BRITE Center praised Argos's personalized cancer treatments and local hiring pipeline. Council members commended Durham County's matching contribution and praised the agreement as a strong use of public capital, approving it 6-0 by voice vote after the electronic voting system failed to register.

votes.item_title: Item 7: Montclair Phase II — Utility Extension, Voluntary Annexation, and Initial Zoning (PDR 2.00 / RR)
votes.notes: Approves utility extension, voluntary annexation, and PDR 2.00/RR zoning for 14.89 acres (up to 24 single-family homes).
votes.discussion_detail: Planning's Pat Young presented the utility extension, voluntary annexation, and initial PDR 2.00 and RR zoning for 14.89 acres at Barbee Chapel and Farrington Mill Roads for up to 24 single-family homes, correcting a typographical date in the annexation ordinance to March 31, 2014. Applicant representative Jared Edens (for David Weekley Homes) proffered $1,500 to Durham Public Schools ($500 per projected student) and a 25-foot undisturbed buffer—15 feet wider than required—instead of the 1,000-foot chain-link fence sought by adjacent farmer Michael Hining. Hining opposed approval without the fence, warning that doubling nearby homes increased the risk of children trespassing into his ponds and over 50 fruit trees. After Edens agreed to shift the school payment deadline to prior to first final plat and Council Member Steve Schewel acknowledged the difficulty of weighing the fence request, Council approved all three actions 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 8: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Meadows at Southpoint II (A1300007)
votes.notes: Amends Future Land Use Map for 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from Office/Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case A1300007 on behalf of Meadows Land Investment LLC to change the Future Land Use Map designation for 46.9 acres at the southeast corner of NC 54 and Barbee Road from Office and Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential, noting a 13-1 approval recommendation from the Planning Commission. George Bryan, speaking for the Hunter's Wood neighborhood, expressed strong support and thanked the applicant for accommodating neighbors' request for residential land use. Applicant attorney Ken Spaulding likewise thanked the neighborhood, Planning Commission, and staff. After closing the public hearing, Council approved the Comprehensive Plan amendment unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 9: Zoning Map Change — Meadows at Southpoint II (Z1300020)
votes.notes: Rezones 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from RR and OI to PDR 4.718 for max 185 residential units.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case Z1300020 rezoning 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road to PDR 4.718 for up to 185 residential units, detailing commitments including stormwater pond aeration, a 100-foot natural perimeter buffer, NC 54 bike-lane pavement, a bus shelter, and roadway improvements. Neighborhood representative George Bryan and applicant attorney Ken Spaulding endorsed the revised townhome plan, though Bryan urged converting the full-access Barbee Road driveway to right-in/right-out or adding warning signs; Transportation's Bill Judge explained sight distance to the left meant right-in/right-out would not fix the issue and NCDOT would enforce sight-distance documentation and signage at construction approval. Following up on Mayor Bell's January 6 request, Council Member Diane Catotti asked to remove vinyl siding, and applicant Jim Anderson and George Stancil agreed to prohibit vinyl siding (using cementitious siding) while keeping vinyl windows. Council Member Steve Schewel also secured a $500 school-mitigation proffer at site plan approval before Council voted 6-0 to approve the rezoning.

disagreements.issue: Montclair Phase II Boundary: 1,000-Foot Chain-Link Fence vs. 25-Foot Undisturbed Buffer (Item 7)
disagreements.summary: Adjacent property owner Michael Hining urged Council to reject Montclair Phase II unless the developer built a 1,000-foot chain-link fence separating the subdivision from his 12-acre farm, whereas the developer refused the fence and offered a 25-foot undisturbed buffer.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the shared property line without requiring a chain-link fence.
side_a_arguments: A chain-link fence is ineffective because people can climb over or walk around it, and law enforcement already addresses trespassing.
Requiring fences along every property line with potential foot traffic would set an unworkable precedent across Durham.
A 25-foot undisturbed buffer adds 15 feet beyond the 10-foot code minimum and benefits both the neighbor and new homeowners (Jared Edens for David Weekley Homes).
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning unless the developer installs a chain-link fence along the 1,000-foot boundary.
side_b_arguments: The neighboring 12-acre farm contains ponds and over 50 fruit trees that pose an attractive nuisance and child safety hazard.
Phase II doubles the nearby housing count and number of children, and a 25-foot buffer or no-trespassing signs will not stop children from entering the farm (Michael Hining).
disagreements.resolution: While Council Member Steve Schewel acknowledged struggling with the request, Council accepted the 25-foot undisturbed buffer proffer and approved Montclair Phase II 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Length and Scope of Downtown Resident Parking Fee Phase-Out (Item 5)
disagreements.summary: Downtown residents, council members, and the City Attorney debated whether early downtown residents could retain free or discounted parking, how long a half-rate phase-in should last, and whether post-2008 residents could be excluded.
disagreements.side_a_position: Provide an extended multi-year half-price phase-in for current downtown residents (Don Moffitt initially favored 10 years, plus surface-lot rate relief; Coke Ariail/Kate Dobbs sought preservation of free parking).
side_a_arguments: Early downtown homeowners bought properties relying on city promises of free parking and helped revitalize downtown and grow property tax receipts (William 'Coke' Ariail, Kate Dobbs).

Charging full rates immediately asks ~130 downtown residents—who already pay higher downtown tax rates—for an extra $100,000/year, and Main Street residents prefer surface parking for safety (Don Moffitt).
disagreements.side_b_position: Limit subsidies to pre-2008 'pioneer' residents if legally possible, or keep the phase-out brief to avoid larger revenue losses.
side_b_arguments: Residents moving in after 2008 were aware of changing policies and should not receive the same long-term subsidy as the ~21 original pioneers (Steve Schewel).
Extending the 50% discount beyond three years costs the city approximately $50,000 in foregone revenue per additional year (clarified by Diane Catotti).
Legally, a retroactive 2008 cutoff would be arbitrary and capricious, leaving a uniform phase-out for all current residents as the only defensible option (City Attorney).
disagreements.resolution: Council compromised 6-0 on Don Moffitt's motion, seconded by Steve Schewel, adopting Option 2 with a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting January 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: At its first meeting of 2014, following a 5:30 p.m. closed session, Mayor Bill Bell announced that the Durham City Council voted unanimously pursuant to NCGS 160A-168(c)(7) to concur with City Manager Tom Bonfield's decision to release a summary report of the Durham Police Department's Internal Affairs investigation into the November 19, 2013 death of Jesus Huerta, while awaiting the pending SBI and medical examiner reports. Council deferred the Meadows at Southpoint II hearings to January 21 due to a newspaper notice error (with Mayor Bell flagging opposition to vinyl siding), adopted the Consent Agenda excluding pulled Items 8 and 9, and approved both pulled items (the SystemVision energy agreement and transferring two city lots to Habitat for Humanity) 7-0. During the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan public hearing (received 7-0), speakers pressed for youth job training, permanent supportive housing, and Northeast Central Durham investment, and CAARE Inc.'s Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged Continuum of Care scoring procedures—prompting Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden to demand a full investigation at Thursday's work session.

agenda_items.title: Committee Appointments and Unanimous Closed-Session Action to Release Jesus Huerta Internal Affairs Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell welcomed Webelos Cub Scouts Pack 400, noted Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden's birthday wishes, and announced Crime Cabinet appointments with Eugene Brown as co-chair, Don Moffitt as member, and Eddie Davis as alternate. Mayor Bell then reported that in a 5:30 p.m. closed session, Council voted unanimously under NCGS 160A-168(c)(7) to concur with City Manager Tom Bonfield's recommendation to release a written summary of DPD's Internal Affairs investigation into the November 19, 2013 death of Jesus Huerta later that week (first sharing it with the family's attorney), while noting the separate SBI investigation remained pending the medical examiner's report.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items: Defer Items 16 and 17 (Meadows at Southpoint II) to January 21, 2014
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested deferring Item 16 (Comprehensive Plan Amendment, Meadows at Southpoint 2) and Item 17 (Zoning Map Change, Meadows at Southpoint 2) to January 21, 2014 due to a newspaper advertisement notification error, which Council approved 7-0. Mayor Bell noted he would miss the January 21 meeting for the U.S. Conference of Mayors and asked colleagues to examine the project's construction materials and prohibit vinyl siding.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 8 and 9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 14 covering council minutes, Appearance Commission and Durham Housing Authority appointments, the memorial resolution for Joseph Becton, Jr., November 2013 bid report, street acceptances, Clover Hill Place paving preliminary assessment roll, SystemVision agreement (Item 8, questioned by Mayor Bell), Habitat for Humanity lot transfer (Item 9, pulled), pumper truck and loader truck purchases, asphaltic concrete extension, Upper Neuse River Basin Association nutrient credit project, and household hazardous waste contract amendment #5. Items 8 and 9 were pulled for separate action and the rest approved 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan Needs Public Hearing (CDBG, HOME, and ESG)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers opened the first required public hearing for the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan, estimating $1.65M in CDBG, $700K in HOME, and $100K in ESG funds. Five speakers testified: Steve Hopkins (jobs, crime prevention, unpaved streets like Hardy St, and protecting Northeast Central Durham residents from displacement), Sharon Elliott-Bynum of CAARE Inc. (disputing Continuum of Care/HSAC funding recommendation scores for a homeless female veterans house and an unreceived 2008-09 $28,000 award), Dwaine Langley of the CAC (homelessness rising to 759, high rents, workforce training, and transit-corridor housing), Debbie White of CASA (permanent supportive housing saving Medicaid costs and CASA's 21.5-year waitlist), and Victoria Peterson (residential youth job training). Community Development Director Reginald Johnson clarified Ms. Bynum's complaints fell under the separate CoC/HSAC process, and Mayor Pro Tempore Cole-McFadden demanded a Thursday work-session investigation while Council Member Steve Schewel asked about CASA's Guess Road project and highlighted the penny-for-housing fund before Council voted 7-0 to receive the comments.

agenda_items.title: SystemVision Program Agreement (NCHFA, City of Durham, and Advanced Energy Corporation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell explained he pulled Item 8 solely for informational clarification regarding Advanced Energy Corporation's guarantee to pay energy cost differences above $33 per month and whether Utility cost inflation was factored in. Staff confirmed the state Housing Finance Agency had long used the company and that Durham used the exact same program in Eastway, satisfying Mayor Bell before Council approved Item 8.

agenda_items.title: Ownership Transfer of Two City-Owned Lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council took up Item 9 regarding the transfer of two city-owned lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc. After brief confirmation involving the acronym CRO and determining the person who pulled the item did not wish to speak further, Council approved the transfer 7-0. Prior to adjourning at 7:48 p.m., Mayor Bell asked Police Chief Lopez and General Services for clarification on the policy governing floral memorials placed on police department property.

votes.item_title: Concurrence with City Manager to Release DPD Internal Affairs Summary on the Death of Jesus Huerta (NCGS 160A-168(c)(7))
votes.notes: Voted unanimously in the 5:30 p.m. closed session prior to the regular meeting and announced in open session by Mayor Bill Bell.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell explained that the regular meeting began slightly late because Council held a 5:30 p.m. closed session regarding the November 19, 2013 death of Jesus Huerta (transcribed as 'Azu Werter' in ASR). In that closed session, Council received an oral summary of the Durham Police Department's Internal Affairs investigation and voted unanimously 7-0 pursuant to N.C. General Statute 160A-168(c)(7) to concur with City Manager Tom Bonfield's determination that releasing the IA findings was essential to maintaining public confidence in city services. Mayor Bell stated a written summary report would be provided to the Huerta family's attorney and released publicly later that week, no later than Friday. He emphasized that the separate State Bureau of Investigation criminal probe awaited the medical examiner's report and would go to the District Attorney rather than Council or DPD.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Items: Defer Items 16 and 17 (Meadows at Southpoint II) to January 21, 2014
votes.notes: Deferred Item 16 (A1300007) and Item 17 (Z1300020) to January 21, 2014 due to a newspaper advertisement notification error.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield reported two priority items requesting deferral of Agenda Item 16 (Comprehensive Plan Amendment, Meadows at Southpoint 2) and Agenda Item 17 (Zoning Map Change, Meadows at Southpoint 2) to the January 21, 2014 meeting due to notification errors in newspaper advertisements. Council properly moved, seconded, and approved the deferrals 7-0. Following the vote, Mayor Bell noted he would be absent on January 21 for the U.S. Conference of Mayors annual meeting and asked council colleagues to scrutinize the project's proposed building materials on page 11 of the packet, urging them to disallow vinyl siding.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-7 and 10-14, Excluding Pulled Items 8 and 9)
votes.notes: Adopted Items 1-7 and 10-14; Item 8 (SystemVision) and Item 9 (Habitat for Humanity lot transfer) were pulled for separate votes.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bell read the titles of Consent Agenda Items 1 through 14, including minutes, Appearance Commission and DHA Board appointments, the memorial resolution for Joseph W. A. Becton, Jr., the November 2013 bid report, street acceptances, the Clover Hill Place street-paving preliminary assessment roll, piggyback and cooperative purchases of a pumper truck and three knuckleboom loader trucks, an asphaltic concrete contract extension, the Upper Neuse River Basin Association nutrient credit project, and household hazardous waste contract amendment #5. Item 8 was set aside for a question from Mayor Bell and Item 9 was pulled by another speaker. A motion to approve the remaining Consent Agenda items was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Receive Public Comments on FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan Needs (CDBG, HOME, ESG)
votes.notes: Action requested by Community Development Department was solely to receive citizen comments for incorporation into the draft Annual Action Plan.
votes.discussion_detail: Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers briefed Council on the first required public hearing for the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan, projecting $1.65 million in CDBG, $700,000 in HOME, and $100,000 in ESG funds. Public speakers Steve Hopkins, Dwaine Langley (CAC), Debbie White (CASA), and Victoria Peterson called for investments in jobs and street paving in Northeast Central Durham, permanent supportive housing to curb healthcare costs and address CASA's 21.5-year waitlist, transit-corridor affordable housing, and residential youth job training. Sharon Elliott-Bynum of CAARE Inc. raised formal process complaints alleging her homeless female veterans project scored higher (85) with the CAC than a recommended renewal project (84) and questioning an unreceived 2008-09 award of $28,000. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson clarified Ms. Bynum's funding fell under the separate Continuum of Care/Homeless Services Advisory Committee process, though Mayor Bell requested follow-up and Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden urged a Thursday work-session investigation; Council Member Steve Schewel also noted the city's $1 million penny-for-housing fund before Council voted 7-0 to receive the comments.

votes.item_title: Item 8 (Pulled): SystemVision Program Agreement (NCHFA, City of Durham, and Advanced Energy Corporation)
votes.notes: Pulled by Mayor Bill Bell solely for informational questions on Advanced Energy Corporation's $33/month utility-cost guarantee.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell explained he had flagged Item 8 to ask about the City's prior experience with Advanced Energy Corporation under the North Carolina Housing Finance Agency's SystemVision program, specifically how often the company had to pay out under its guarantee covering energy costs exceeding $33 per month and whether utility rate increases affected that threshold. Staff replied that NCHFA had partnered with the company for years and that Durham used the exact same program and contractor in the Eastway development, promising follow-up data on past payout frequency. Satisfied with the track record in Eastway, Mayor Bell moved approval of Item 8. After a second, Council passed the agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 9 (Pulled): Ownership Transfer of Two City-Owned Lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc.
votes.notes: Pulled item taken up after public hearings; person who pulled the item did not speak further and Council approved 7-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Council turned to pulled Consent Item 9 transferring ownership of two city-owned lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc. Following a brief exchange clarifying the acronym CRO and noting that the individual who had pulled the item was no longer pursuing comments, Mayor Bell entertained a motion to approve. A motion and second were made without further debate. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the property transfer.

disagreements.issue: Continuum of Care / Homeless Funding Scoring Fairness and Transparency (Item 15)
disagreements.summary: During the Annual Action Plan public hearing, nonprofit leader Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged the fairness and transparency of Community Development's Continuum of Care funding recommendations, prompting Council scrutiny despite staff explaining it was a separate process from CDBG/HOME/ESG.
disagreements.side_a_position: Investigate and reform funding recommendations to ensure fair scoring, process clarity, and inclusion of smaller/new nonprofits such as female veterans housing.
side_a_arguments: CAARE Inc.'s proposal to rehab a home for four homeless female veterans scored an average of 85 from the Citizens Advisory Committee compared to 84 for the staff-recommended agency, yet was passed over (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).
The recommended project was part two of a renewal rather than a new project, and an earlier $28,000 award from 2008-09 was never disbursed after the prior director's death (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).

Council must fully investigate the process at Thursday's work session because having the same organizations receive funding repeatedly does not appear fair (Cora Cole-McFadden; follow-up also requested by Bill Bell).
disagreements.side_b_position: Clarify that Continuum of Care recommendations follow a separate HUD process overseen by the Homeless Services Advisory Committee rather than the CDBG/HOME/ESG Annual Action Plan.
side_b_arguments: The funding cited by Ms. Bynum comes from the Continuum of Care process scheduled before the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, which makes recommendations separately from the Annual Action Plan hearing (Community Development Director Reginald Johnson).
Staff would research the historical $28,000 award question separately.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to receive all public hearing comments while directing Community Development staff to investigate Ms. Bynum's complaints and report back at Thursday's work session.
